title: Roncus bavierai Gardini & Gardini, 2026, sp. nov.
abstract: Roncus bavierai sp. nov. (Figs 39–47, 114) Type locality: Italy, Sicily, Palermo Province, Piana degli Albanesi, Monte Pizzuta, Grotta del Garrone 160 Si/PA (38°00’09”N 13°15’57”E). Distribution. Italy (Sicily). Diagnosis (♂ ♀). A small-sized highly troglomorphic Roncus that differs from other Sicilian species of the genus in the following combination of characters: carapace without eyes or eye spots, with triangular epistome, posterior border with 6 setae; tergite I with 6 setae; cheliceral palm with 6 setae; anterior margin of genital opening of male with 38 setae; pedipalpal femur and chelal hand with a moderately granular surface, patella smooth; pedipalpal femur gradually clavate, 1.03–1.18 mm length (5.02–5.15 ×), without tubercles on the paraxial face; patella with elongated club with subparallel sides, 0.83–0.98 mm (3.25–3.38 ×), club/pedicel ratio = 1.62–1.65; chelal hand with no microsetae both proximal to the trichobothrium eb and between eb-esb; fixed and movable chelal fingers with 98–110 and 102–108 teeth, respectively; 34–35 teeth between the trichobothrium t and the apex of the movable chelal finger; movable chelal finger 1.15–1.33 mm length; ratio of movable chelal finger/hand of chela with pedicel 1.53–1.60; ratio of pedipalpal femur/movable chelal finger lengths 0.88–0.89; ratio of pedipalpal femur/carapace 1.21–1.32. Type material. ITALY — Sicily: Palermo Province: 1♀ holotype (not treated with lactic acid), Piana degli Albanesi, Monte Pizzuta, Grotta del Garrone 160 Si/PA, 1100 m a.s.l., 5.IV.2013, P. Magrini leg. (MHNG); Paratypes: 1♂ 1♀ (in poor condition), same data as holotype but 4.IV.2011, P. Magrini leg. (coll. G. Gardini, Genoa). Derivatio nominis. Dedicated to Cosimo Baviera (University of Messina) in gratitude for having provided the numerous pseudoscorpion specimens collected during his careful and repeated fieldwork throughout Sicily. Description of adults (♂ ♀). Carapace, chelicerae, pedipalps and palpal coxae yellowish; pedipalpal femur and chelal hand with moderately granular surface, patella smooth, pleural membrane granulate. Carapace 1.43–1.54 (♂ ♀) times as long as broad, anterior margin with triangular epistome apically blunt; no eyes or eye spots (Fig. 39); anterior lateral process obtuse, not prominent; weak subbasal transverse furrow present; chaetotaxy 4:8:6:6, subocular setae absent. Chaetotaxy of tergites I–X (♂ ♀): 6:9–10:11:11–12:11:11:11:11:11:9 Chaetotaxy of sternites II–X (♂): 38:(3)10?(3):(3)10(3):15:13:14:13:13:12, lateral and median genital sacs not seen, genital atrium with 2+2 setae; genital area as in fig. 41, anterior margin of genital opening with 38 (!) setae; chaetotaxy of sternites II–IX (♀): 9:(3)14(3):(3)12(3):13:14:14:14:12. Chelicera 2.00–2.03 (♂ ♀) times as long as broad, palm with 6 setae; fixed and movable cheliceral finger with about 10–15 (worn) teeth; movable finger with the largest tooth just distad gs; gs ratio 0.64–0.66, spinneret barely noticeable in both sexes; rallum with one short proximal blade and 7 or 8 longer blades, all blades anteriorly combed, also the first, which is apparently smooth; serrulae interior and exterior with about 28 and 30 blades, respectively. Manducatory process with 4 setae. Coxal setae (♂ ♀): pedipalp 7, I 7–8, II 7, III 5, IV 8; anterolateral process of coxa I stubby and pointed, anteromedial process not prominent, rounded (Fig. 40). Pedipalp (Figs 42–47): trochanter 2.50–2.85 (♂ ♀) times as long as broad, with a tubercle with lyrifissure on antiaxial face; femur 5.02 (♂) or 5.15 (♀) times as long as broad, gradually enlarged from the base, tubercles on the paraxial face absent, granulation as in figs 42, 45; patella with smooth surface, 3.38 (♂) or 3.25 (♀) times as long as broad, with one weak dorso-distal tubercle with glandular pore and one or three micropores at base of dorsal face of pedicel; club/pedicel ratio of patella (♂ ♀) = 1.60–1.65; chela with pedicel 4.55 (♂) or 4.58 (♀) times as long as broad [4.94 (♂) or 4.77 (♀) times as long as deep]; hand of chela with pedicel 1.84 (♂) or 1.92 (♀) times as long as broad [2.0 (♂ ♀) times as long as deep], with oval profile and its greatest width in the proximal third (dorsal view), granulation as in figs 43–44, 46–47; chelal hand with a tubercle with a glandular pore on the antiaxial face close to the movable finger base and one micropore at base of dorsal face of pedicel; microsetae between the trichobothria eb and esb and microsetae proximal eb absent (Figs 44, 47); fixed chelal finger with 110 (♂) or 98 (♀) contiguous and weakly pointed teeth; nodus ramosus subterminal; movable chelal finger with 108 (♂) or 102 (♀) teeth (8–9 teeth occupying 0.1 mm) with flat apex teeth, apart from the distals which are pointed (Figs 44, 47); 34–35 teeth between the trichobothrium t and the apex of the movable finger; marginal sensillum at the level of the trichobothrium sb; all teeth with dental canals; trichobothria as in figs 43–44, 46–47, relative position of trichobothria along chelal axis (♂ ♀): et 0.14–0.17/ it 0.225 –0.265 / est 0.30 –0.31/ ist 0.425–0.45/ isb 0.665–0.70/ ib 0.84/ esb 0.905–0.91/ eb 0.95– 0.96/ t 0.24–0.26/ st 0.41–0.42/ sb 0.655–0.72/ b 0.87–0.88; trichobothrium isb closer to ib than to ist, trichobothrium est closer to t than to st; ratio of movable chelal finger/hand of chela with pedicel 1.60 (♂) or 1.53 (♀); ratio of pedipalpal femur/movable finger 0.88 (♂) or 0.89 (♀); ratio of pedipalpal femur and carapace 1.32 (♂) or 1.21 (♀). Leg IV: trochanter 2.27 (♀) times as long as deep, femur + patella 4.04 (♀) times as long as deep, tibia 6.83 (♀) times (TS = 0.64), basitarsus 3.15 (♀) times (TS = 0.18), telotarsus 5.41 (♀) times as long as deep (TS = 0.38), ratio of basitarsus/telotarsus 0.65 (♀), subterminal seta furcate, claws with dorsal tooth. Measurements. Body length 2.25 (♀). Carapace 0.89 × 0.62 anteriorly (♂) or 0.85 × 0.55 anteriorly (♀). Chelicera 0.56 × 0.28 (♂) or 0.54 × 0.265 (♀); movable finger length 0.385 (♂) or 0.36 (♀). Pedipalp: trochanter 0.60 × 0.24 (♂) or 0.57 × 0.20 (♀); femur 1.18 × 0.235 (♂) or 1.03 × 0.20 (♀); patella 0.98 × 0.29 (♂) or 0.83 × 0.255 (♀); chela with pedicel 2.05 × 0.45 (depth 0.415) (♂) or 1.79 × 0.39 (depth 0.375) (♀); hand with pedicel length 0.83 (♂) or 0.75 (♀); movable finger length 1.33 (♂) or 1.15 (♀). Leg IV: trochanter 0.375 × 0.165 (♀); femur + patella 0.89 × 0.22 (♀); tibia 0.82 × 0.12 (♀); basitarsus 0.30 × 0.095 (♀); telotarsus 0.46 × 0.085 (♀). Remarks. The affinities of Roncus bavierai sp. nov. remain unknown at present. This small species, which is highly specialised to the subterranean habitat, exhibit several distinctive characteristics that are not found in any of the other known Sicilian―or even Sardinian― Roncus. The chelal fingers are more than one and a half times as long as the hand [ratio between movable finger and hand of chela with pedicel lengths 1.60 (♂) or 1.53 (♀)] and have a very high number of teeth in relation to the fingers size [fixed chelal finger with 110 (♂) or 98 (♀), movable chelal finger with 108 (♂) or 102 (♀) teeth; movable chelal finger with 8–9 teeth occupying 0.1 mm]. In addition, the pedipalpal femur is shorter than the movable chelal finger (femur/finger ratio 0.88–0.89) and the male genital operculum (sternite II) bears a dense cluster of 38 setae (Fig. 41), whereas all other Sicilian species have no more than 27.

title: Artshack : (balance, chaos and ambiguity)
abstract:
The initial idea of constructing Artshack was to create a small, functional art studio. During the process of building it I felt I was creating something special. The framework is irregular and uneven giving Artshack a quality of motion and instability. I made the windows various sizes, shapes and tilted at different angles to suggest unevenness and irregularity. As a result, shafts of light flood in from different directions, reflecting, illuminating and defining the interior with a luminous quality. The interior colors are mat and neutral in nature so as not to distract from the works on display. Yet the exterior is painted with bright, cheerful colors which makes it stand out from the other structures in the area. The cactus plants surrounding the structure outside are symbolic of survival in any situation. The project had evolved into a form of painted sculptural expression as well as very personal space similar to a small chapel. It has ultimately become a place for me to be alone, free of external restraints and stimulation. A place to focus, meditate, tune in and connect with creative energy, where the mind can soar and give birth to creativity. 
I shall attempt here to verbalize a personal philosophy that affects my artistic vision. It is primarily visual and emphasizes the use of feelings, emotion and intuition. Its foundation is spiritual in nature. The basic concept is concerned with the duality of nature, polarity or action and reaction, light and darkness, day and night, male and female, good and evil, and yin and yang. Everything that exists has a duality that cuts it into two equal and opposite paths. Each half suggests another to make it whole. The universe is represented in every one of its molecules. ???while the universe at large is dur1J in nature, so is ever; one of its parts. The absolute balance of give and take, right and wrong. Our strength lies in our weaknesses. Every inside has an outside, every ray of light has a shadow. We cannot divide things in half and only accept one side. The other half will strive until it has found its opposite and completed a whole. A person cannot do wrong without suffering wrong. Every excess causes a defect. Every defect an excess. Every good has its evil. We tend to focus on weaknesses, but it is the strength that shines through. 
The spiral construction outside the Artshack that penetrates the structure and reemerges into space symbolizes new life, death and the oneness of the universe at large. Its intention is to illustrate the balance, chaos, and ambiguity that exists in our immediate environment and the cosmos. The Cobra, outside the Artshack, and many of the snake forms inside are symbolic of the struggle against one's self and society to free self-expression and the birth of creativity. It is my belief that evil or the dark side is our alter ego, the side of us that it is not accepted by our society, but in reality exists, and it has materialized itself in many of the works. 
My work attempts to embody the concepts of balance, chaos, and ambiguity. Balance in this case signifies the yang, which gives structure, logic and stability to the works. It is the subtle energy that provides balance in nature. Chaos is defined as the irregular, dark side, embodying the yin in nature, which is responsible for purity, and the child like innocence represented in nature. These two subtle opposite and equal forces meet to give rise to various creations that are ambiguous in nature and embody constant change that is the only absolute. The work in the center is composed of castings of the artist's decaying face and hands, covered with scorpions, frogs, insects and worms, signifying change in life and ultimately, death. 
An oil painting of a nun-like woman in prayer which signifies the female spiritual nature is directly across from a ceramic demon-Medussa head submerged in water symbolizing evil and the alter ego coming into material existence. There are many animal figures, landscape paintings, and related works in different media which symbolize creations of nature. In one corner, a small alter contains a bronze goddess figure which symbolizes Mother Earth. The other surrounding works all pay tribute to her and signify dignity of the Earth while giving less emphasis to the male side, giving a sense of balance and equilibrium. The intention is to create a holistic feeling in the total environment of Artshack with each piece contributing to the whole and making it a complete work. 
The works inside or outside the Artshack speak for themselves. They may make no sense in terms of the viewer's personal experiences, however, viewers have the freedom to respond to the works with their own interpretations and give new, personal, meanings to them. In other words, the works become a vehicle of creativity in the viewer's mind. 
To me, the process of creation is a ritual, it is an act of reverence to nature and everything encompassing it. It involves detachment and self-liberation from constraint, social taboos and universal truths. Many of the works I have created and presented here are very different from one another, yet, I believe that there is a common thread that unites their eclectic qualities in the presence of spirituality, peace of mind, and tranquility. 
The presence of Artshack, is essentially a state of mind that brings together the basis of all creation, the polarities that dictate life and everything that surrounds us, the unique wholeness of each individual to the oneness of the universe. It is a universe in itself detached yet a part of the whole that makes it complete. It is that balance that keeps us sane and happy. Any imbalance causes one side to grow stronger and in so doing weakens the other half. This is the law of the universe and to go with the flow of things and not against them is my personal goal.

title: Foreword: Th e Visitors’ Question
abstract: Th e Visitors' Question carter wilson for fifteen years, most of my opportunities to see the plays of the Monkey Business Th eatre, Teatro Lo'il Maxil, have come about through the happy coincidence of being where the company was performing at the right moment.As a friend of cofounder Robert M. Laughlin and several of the original actors, I have always kept an eye on the performance's eff ect on the spectators, whether the show is Torches for a New Dawn presented in the plaza of Zinacantán for Mayan schoolchildren or Rogelio Román Hernández Cruz's Th e World Turned on Its Head acted before a glittery overfl ow crowd in the Salón Manuel Ponce at Mexico City's Palace of Fine Arts.At the Th eatre's San Cristóbal de las Casas headquarters in 2000, one select audience was made up of eight or nine North American indigenous artistsactors, dancers, poets, and a director-traveling together through southern Mexico to better acquaint themselves with Mayan culture, ancient and present-day.Th e room was not large, barely space enough for the backdrop curtain, the stage action, and some hard wooden chairs for the guests.Th e show Monkey Business presented that afternoon was When Corn Was Born, which features the fearsome red-coated Earth Lord, a scorpion, and a scad of scurrying ants played by fi nger puppets, plus kibbitzing and a helping hand for the poor humans of the piece from two of the ancient Mayan gods, portrayed by actors' voices and huge puppet heads peering down from above the backdrop.Several of the visitors had been trained in New York and were acquainted with the style of Ralph Lee, who had been coming annually to develop and stage a play with Monkey Business Th eatre.In the discussion following the performance, the guests asked how much of what they had just seen was Ralph Lee and how much came out of the troupe's own indigenous traditions.At fi rst, the actors did not answer.Th e question seemed to have generated some tension, as though the guests had reservations about what they had [ x ] monkey business theatre just seen.Th en company member Juan de la Torre made a short speech, pointing out that the Maya have preserved their languages and culture through the more than fi ve hundred years since the arrival of the European invaders.And this they have done, he said, in the face of heavy opposition and disrespect, and with virtually no help from government agencies or other outside sources.Juan's speech pleased the Native American artists.Th ey began off ering songs in their own languages as thanks to the Monkey Business actors, and then there was an exchange of handshakes and abrazos all around.Most people in the outside world are aware that the ancient Maya had a fully functional writing system based on glyphs, and many may know that the modern descendants of the Maya maintain a rich oral story culture.But they know less about Mayan literacy, written literature, and dramatic traditions, either in the deep past or the present.Th e following brief sketch of this heritage provides a good introduction to the Monkey Business Th eatre's fi rst collection of plays, especially since, even though they usually perform in Spanish, Monkey Business is an important contributor to a vital movement to revive Mayan literacy and literature and to keep Mayan culture vital.-On a July day in 1562, less than fi fty years into the Spanish occupation of the Yucatán Peninsula, Friar Diego de Landa, a Franciscan, had fi ve thousand Mayan idols destroyed at the town of Maní and burned the twenty-seven Mayan books he could lay his hands on.Th ough Landa could not read the texts, he was convinced they must be full of lies perpetrated by the Devil.At the time, Landa's newly converted Indian fl ock "regretted" the destruction of their books "to an amazing degree," as Landa noted.It caused them, he said, "great affl iction."Th e Mayan glyphic writing system was a key accomplishment of a civilization that was nearly two thousand years old when the Spanish came along.No one really knows how many people in the Mayas' city-states could actually read and write, but archaeologists think maybe only 2 percent could write, most of them men, but some women as well.Nevertheless, the relatively small number who were literate were key contributors to social life and included not only ruling lords and ladies, but also the astronomers who interpreted the past in order to predict the future, prized artisans, the medical practitioners who could divine your illness and cast it from your body, the storytellers, and probably some of the professional entertainers.Friar Landa reported that those who could read and write did not always tout their skill in public, but they would have books buried with them, presumably so they could use them again in the next life.

title: Against Autobiography: Albert Memmi and the Production of Theory par Lia Nicole Brozgal
abstract: African characters, while also noting the novelist’s tendency to echo without question the era’s predominant ideology of the mission civilisatrice. These issues would seem directly pertinent to a discussion of Verne’s role in forming the worldview of fin de siècle France. One would like to see the implications of these questions developed in greater depth, rather than dismissed with offhand comments such as “Ce n’est pas encore le ‘United Colors of Benetton’” (28). The shallowness of Jules Verne: un océan tumultueux de mots et de rêves limits its usefulness. Yet the book’s second section, “Résumé commenté,” is rather fun. It showcases Boumahdi’s strength (descriptive breadth rather than analytic depth), and it gives the reader a sense of the cumulative weight of Verne’s nearly eighty works of fiction. It may serve as an encyclopedic (or Wikipedic) reference tool. Arcadia University (PA) Kate M. Bonin Brozgal, Lia Nicole. Against Autobiography: Albert Memmi and the Production of Theory. Lincoln: UP of Nebraska, 2013. ISBN 978-0-8032-4042-1. Pp. xxvi + 223. $50. À partir du postulat selon lequel les œuvres francophones du Maghreb sont souvent lues comme des textes ethnographiques ou autobiographiques, c’est-à-dire comme des représentations “authentiques” (23), Brozgal avance que la “mort de l’auteur” de Barthes n’a pas eu lieu en francophonie puisque la critique ne cesse de revenir aux intentions, à la “race” et à l’identité sexuée (gender) de l’écrivain. Malgré son titre, ce n’est toutefois pas contre l’autobiographie comme genre littéraire qu’elle prend position, mais plutôt contre“an interpretative lens or reading strategy”(xiii) qui néglige la richesse du corpus francophone. L’auteure étudie les stratégies narratives, discursives et para-textuelles qui sont à l’œuvre dans les essais autant que dans les romans d’Albert Memmi et souligne la porosité des genres et des discours dans la “production de la théorie”. Cet aspect constitue l’intérêt et l’originalité de ce livre, car s’il est en effet connu que le Portrait du colonisé, précédé du portrait du colonisateur de Memmi—dans lequel il tient compte de la totalité du contexte colonial en ce qu’il analyse les effets de la “maladie” qu’est la colonisation sur le colonisé et sur le colonisateur—s’inscrit dans une réflexion théorique postcoloniale, Brozgal montre que ses romans participent également aux“lieux de la théorie”, subvertissant ainsi ces catégories supposément étanches. Outre le chapitre sur le regard, la vision et l’aveuglement dans La statue de sel et Le scorpion, une attention particulière est portée aux enjeux régulièrement soulevés en études francophones: le concept de“francophonie” (que Memmi abordait déjà avec vigilance en 1985 sans cependant en sonner le glas comme l’a fait un certain manifeste publié dans Le Monde en 2007), les théories postcoloniales, l’approche féministe, la réception et les instances de légitimation. Par une lecture attentive des célèbres préfaces de Sartre, qui ont contribué à la légitimation 212 FRENCH REVIEW 89.2 Reviews 213 d’essais francophones tout en leur faisant de l’ombre, Brozgal met en lumière les différentes postures: tout se passe comme si Sartre se voulait l’intermédiaire entre le lecteur français et les poèmes de l’Anthologie de Senghor et solidaire à l’appel à la libération des Damnés de la terre de Fanon, mais que sa préface au Portrait du colonisé de Memmi (qui est en fait un compte rendu d’abord paru dans Les Temps modernes) n’était qu’un prétexte à sa propre critique de la colonisation. Consacré au Portrait du colonisé et au Portrait du décolonisé arabo-musulman et de quelques autres, le quatrième chapitre se penche sur un changement considérable: en tant que Tunisien de confession juive, Memmi se situait dans son premier essai à l’intérieur et à l’extérieur du groupe des colonisés, position ambivalente lui permettant de saisir la complexité des rapports coloniaux, alors qu’il se distancie manifestement des...

title: 日本産硬骨魚類における小脳弁の比較解剖学的研究
abstract: The external and internal character of valvula cerebelli in brain was observed for 58 Genus 108 Species of common Japanese Teleost taken from various waters. A comparative anatomic investigation to the phylogenic group relation of these fishes was made by histological method. 1) The size of valvula cerebelli in optic ventricle varies in each species. The valvula cerebelli of angler (Lophius litulon), genuim goby (Acanthogobius flavimanus), nagazuka (Stichaeus grigorjewi), true lizzard fish (Saurus undosquamis), devil stinger (Inimichus japonicus) etc. which live in the bottom of water and which take foods mainly depending on smell sense, is small and occupies only 30 % in length of optic ventricle, and that of anchovy (Engraulis japonica), black porgy (M ylio macroce phalus), mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and dolphin (Cor yphaena hi ppurus) etc. which have well developed accoustic and optic sense centre and which live in surface water, is large and occupies about 60 % in length of optic ventricle. 2) External form, especially dorsal view of valvula cerebelli, also varies by species. The shapes a small projection type like that of pond smelt (Hypomesus olidus), Japanese conger (Astroconger myriaster), hatahata (Arctoscopus japonicus), oya-nirami (Coreoperca kawamebari), ikanago (Ammodytes personatus), hire-guro (G'yptoce phalus stelleri), Pacific cod (Gadus macrocephalus) etc. double type like that of yanagi-mushigarei (Tanakius kitahrai), stone block type like that of Salmonidae and complicated revolved type like that of dolphin (Coryphaena hi ppurus), skipjack (Katsuwonus pelamis), tuna (Thunnus thynnus), suma (Euthynnus affinis yaito), etc .. till further, the valvula cerebelli shows some distinction in shape in the same Family and Genus, and the fish having a complicated type of valvula has a speedy swim- ming behaviour and takes well developed lateral line sense centre better than that of simple type. 3) Internal structure of valvula cerebelli as that of cor pus cerebelli, consists of granular cell layer and molecular cell layer. Both cell layers have the same function as cor pus cerebelli, and afferent and efferent fibres in the brain end in each cell layer. The result of comparing the volumes of the two layers shows that the granular cell layer is well developed in valvula cerebelli of sardine (Sardinops melanosticta), Pacific herring (Clupea pallasi), konoshiro (Konosirus punctatus), black porgy (Mylio macroce phalus) etc. which have accoustic behaviour and surface swimming habits. On the other hand, the molecular cell layer is larger in ao-mishima (Gnathagnus elongatus), nagazuka (Stichaeus grigor jewi), etc. which mainly has dull motion and bottom feeding habits by smell sense. 4) As Cor pus cerebelli, there are large cells named Purkinje cell in valvula cerebelli of fish and does not form cell layer like other higher vertebrates. This cell lies scattered mainly in the border of the two cell layers of valvula cerebelli. 5) The most fibre tracts which exist in valvula cerebelli are tractus mesence- phalo-cerebellaris anterior, tractus mesence phalo-cerebellaris posterior, tractus laterocerebellaris, tractus secondary gustator y, tractus cerebello-motorius, nervus IVth etc .. 6) Tractus mesencephalo-cerebellaris anterior have close connection with the development of mesencephalon. In optical sense fishes, for example, in the groups of sardine, salmon, mackerel, suzuki etc., tractus mesence phalo-cerebellaris anterior are well dereloped in shape. 7) Tractus mesence phalo-cerebellaris posterior relates with post medulla oblongata and cerebellum. This fibre shows are well developed form of valvula in gropus of sardine, salmon, tuna, mackerel, suzuki and cod which are developed in acoustic sense organ, and in groupes of Cyprinidae, goatfish and flatfish which are developed in central tastal sense organ. 8) There are almost always cases where tractus latero-cerebellaris and tractus secondary gustatory are close with tractus mesence phalo-cerebellaris posterior, so generally do not show in principle. Only in some fishes which have both large accoustic and tastic sence organs can well development in principle be observed. 9). Tractus cerebello-motorius in groups sardine, salmon etc., as well developed, but in the gurnard, scorpion fish and others having dull habit there is less development than others. 10) Nervus IVth in valvula cerevelli is well developed in groups of sardine, salmon, goby, flat fish, cod etc .. 11) In observing the shape of valvula cerebelli from three dimensions instead of the usual dorsal view alone, more variations of shape can be discovered. According to this observation method, valvula cerebelli is classified into two major categories. The one has the simple shape as in case of high-eyes, catfish etc; and the other has the complicated shape, in which there further minor variations. For example, some are biased to the front like in case of konoshiro, sardines, ayu, mullet etc., some are piled as in case of salmon and others, and some are divided into two parts, each having a sperpent like form, as in the case of mackerel, dolphin, tuna, skipjack etc .. 12) If the internal structure of valvula cerebelli is simple, the external shape is also simple, on the other hand those with complicated internal structure show complicated shapes, like complex, revolving or stoneblock shape. 13) Valvula cerebelli of the species having developed cor pus cerebelli shows large shape or complex structure. Contrarily some species having small cor pus cerebelli show small or simple form. 14) The shape and struture of valvula cerebelli show special character of species so it would be possible to distinguish between Family and Genus. 15) 103 species of teleosts were subdivided according to the form and structure of valvula cerebelli for each Order and Sub-order. An index table and phylogenic tree were produced. They are beleived to express the characters of species in another standpoint of the common classification. 16) Valvula cerebelli is developed mainly by crossing portion between cor pus cerebelli and fundus mesence phalis. All cerebellar tracts pass this position and some of these fibre end in the cell layer of the valvula. So it is believed that valvula cerebelli functions by receiving impulses from mesencephalon, medulla oblongata or the spinal cord, and sends another transmision through the body by the spinal cord.

title: [Acaricidal activity of "Medifox" against the human itch mites Sarcoptes scabiei].
abstract: The acaricidal activity of Medifox was evaluated in terms of the itch mites to lend support to the validity of its regimen to treat human scabies. Experiments using mainly females, eggs, and larvae withdrawn from the burrows on the skin of patients with scabies were performed. Permethrin contained in 0.4% aqueous Medifox emulsion was found to affect an itch mite by contact and intestinal routes, without a marked knock-down effect; however, the signs of intoxication are irreversible and lead to the death of Medifox-treated mites. In an in vitro experiment, 100% death of specimens occurred 24-48 hours after immersion of the active stages in the aqueous emulsion for 1 min, depending on the stage of their development. Visual inspection of the course of embryogenesis and the hatch of larvae from eggs under a light microscope established that 20-40-min exposure to Medifox emulsion did not prevent the final formation of a larva and its hatch if the egg was at the late stages of embryogenesis. Long-term (180-min) exposure yielded a 100% ovicidal effect. An in vivo experiment indicated that there were no viable mites in the scabies burrows after single-to-double treatment of patients. Repeated applications are required due to their incomplete ovicidal effect. As a matter of fact, the third treatment is additional to create the "safety factor" of therapy. It is concluded that there is an agreement of the results of in vitro and in vivo experiments, by studying Medifox as an example. The findings suggest that the chosen Medifox treatment regimen including three consecutive treatments results in complete eradication of all the stages of the causative agent on the patient.

VERAGUAS: Santa Fe: El Pantano, 2 juv, 5 April 2017, coll. D. Archibold (CoZEM-ICGES). Diagnosis. Follows Francke & Stockwell (1987) and own data. Total body length ranges from 85 to 105 mm. Colouration: this is a highly polymorphic species. Its colouration varies, with morphs generally appearing in light yellow, reddish, dark brown, or even blackish; the ocular tubercle, the marginal carinae of the carapace, the carinae of the metasoma, telson, segment V of the metasoma, and the digits of the pedipalps are blackish. Carapace: granulation is sparse and fine. Lateral ocular tubercles with three macro-ocelli each. Ocular tubercle with a pair of smooth granular superciliary carinae projecting above the median ocelli. Lateral ocular carinae weak, finely granular. Posterior median carinae are present and weakly granular. Anteromedian furrow is moderately deep; posteromedian furrow is narrow and deep posteriorly; posterolateral furrows are moderately deep and slightly curved; posteromarginal furrow is shallow and wide. Pectines: pectinal tooth count in females varies between 18 to 29 teeth, while males have between 19 and 31; basal plate square. Mesosoma: finely and sparsely granular. Median carinae present in all tergites, weak in tergites I and II, moderate in III-V and fine granular in VI and VII. Tergite VII pentacarinate. Pedipalp: orthobothriotaxic, type A, only sparsely hirsute. All carinae of femur and patella weak to extremely weak granular; internal faces of femur and patella weakly tuberculate. The chela is thin, 4.5 to 5.0 times longer than wide; The chela is almost as wide as the patella, it can be up to 1.3 times wider than the patella. Chela with five carinae: dorsal secondary, dorsal marginal, and ventroexternal carinae weak, feebly granulose; dorsal internal vestigial, granular; digital carina vestigial to obsolete, present as a few basal granules; all other carinae obsolete. Nine main rows of granules in fixed and movable fingers. Fingers of the chela with basal lobe/notch combination moderate. Metasoma: segments of the metasoma with 10-8-8-8-5 carinae consisting of very fine and widely spaced granules. Intercarinal surfaces smooth. segments II–IV with two pairs of ventrolateral macrosetae. The segment V of the metasoma is 2.4 to 2.6 times longer than wide in females and 3 to 3.5 times in males. Telson with vesicle ovate in females, and oval elongate in male. Subaculear tubercle moderate spiniform directed toward the apex of the aculeus. Variation: This species exhibits considerable variability in colouration, total body length, and pectinal tooth count. Reported total body lengths range from 55 to 110 mm (Francke & Stockwell, 1987; Blasco-Aróstegui et al., 2020; Armas & Cubas-Rodríguez, 2023). The male holotype measures 100 mm in total length (Pocock, 1898). In the present study, specimens ranged from 75 to 102 mm in total length. According to Pocock (1898), Francke & Stockwell (1987), Montoya & Armas (2002), and Armas & Cubas-Rodríguez (2023), pectinal tooth counts vary from 18 to 29 in females and from 19 to 31 in males. In the material examined for this study, pectinal tooth counts ranged from 24 to 26 in females and from 25 to 27 in males. Distribution: Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. This includes the island territories of Panama (Bocas del Toro Archipelago) and Honduras (Utila Island), both in the Caribbean Sea (Montoya & Armas, 2002; Armas & Cubas-Rodríguez, 2023). Centruroides limbatus has been reported mostly in secondary forests and areas impacted by human activity throughout its distribution (Blasco-Aróstegui et al., 2020). It is frequently found in banana and oil palm plantations common in the region, in pasture fences, and even in the surroundings and inside human dwellings. Remarks: Centruroides limbatus was compared to Centruroides gracilis since its description (Pocock, 1898). In Panama, Lourenço & Méndez (1984) identified some specimens of C. limbatus from Bocas del Toro as C. gracilis, which we corroborated through a partial review of this material deposited in the CoZEM-ICGES. Montoya & Armas (2002) were the first to report the presence of C. limbatus in Panama, specifically in the Bocas del Toro Archipelago. For their part, Escudero-Sanjur et al. (2022), through phylogenetic analysis based on mitochondrial genes (COI and 16S), obtained that C. limbatus grouped closely with Centruroides gracilis and with C. panamensis. Reproductive biology: Davidson et al. (2020) reported a female of C. limbatus with more than 30 second-stage juveniles from Utila Island in April 2020. In addition, Lezcano et al. (2022) reported that in captivity, C. limbatus produces litters of 34 ± 5 hatchlings (n =7 births) in May and December. Natural history: Prey records for C. limbatus are diverse, and includes: insects (Orthoptera, Blattodea), centipedes (Geophilomorpha, Scolopendromorpha), spiders (Lycosidae, Araneidae, and Theraphosidae).Interactions with other scorpions include reports of intraguild predation on two Tityus species (Miranda et al., 2015; Blasco-Aróstegui et al., 2020) and cannibalism (Blasco-Aróstegui et al., 2020; Armas & Cubas-Rodríguez, 2023). Brown & Arrivillaga (2019) mention a case of cohabitation of a female C. limbatus with the gecko Phyllodactylus palmeus Dixon, 1968 on Utila Island, in the Caribbean of Honduras. Venom and scorpionism: The most abundant fractions of C. limbatus venom display neurotoxic effects when injected intracranially into mice and cause paralysis in insects; however, they are not lethal to mice when administered intraperitoneally (Salazar et al., 2018). Díaz et al. (2025) reported that the venoms of C. limbatus and C. bicolor are very similar and share numerous protein components, including several putative ion channel-modulating toxins. However, they found differences in the efficacy of their venoms against various insect species. Furthermore, these researchers discovered that C. limbatus venom also shares biochemical similarities with that of C. gracilis. title: A popular guide to the observation of nature, or, Hints of inducement to the study of natural productions and appearances, in their connexions and relations / by Robert Mudie.
abstract: The Necessity and Use of Observing.So natural is observation to us, that we in com- mon language allude to it in cases where there is really nothing to observe.When we are perplexed and in difficulty about the absent or the future, and take counsel together in order that, by our union, we may overcome the difficulty, our words of mutual encouragement are, " Let us see ;" and when we have exercised our thoughts rightly, and the difficulty is overcome to our mind, our expression of triumph is, " Now we see our way."Also, when- ever we fail in that which we attempt, or err in the performance of it, the cause of the failure or the error is, that " We do not see our way."To see our way, and to see it clearly, ought therefore, in all matters, to be our very first object.Indeed, the only difference between the ignorant and the intel- ligent is, that the former grope, as it were, in the dark, and the latter see the end of matters, as if the road were open and straight, and the noon-day sun shining upon it.This seeing with the mind this light of the un- P WHY DO WE REMEMBER!when they happened, that the events of our youth return to us in our old age, while those of the more energetic, and therefore more valuable period of our manhood, which, in respect of time, are more recent, are forgotten, and " will not come when we do call them," call with what earnestness we may.As little is it that our judgment is in youth more acute ; for we have seen that the most perfect memory a memory probably more perfect, and certainly more minute, than that of any person of superior intelligence can exist with very little judg-i ment, or with none at all.Is it the novelty then tNo ; not altogether, and probably not at all ; for in that case, we would surely best remember the great- est novelty ; and that unquestionably is the first sight we get of the world.The reason why we remember cannot be explained by the individual things that we remember ; and as little can it be owing to any act of the mind, con- sidered as such.Where then shall we seek for it ?We shall best answer that question by putting another, and pausing to weigh it well before we answer it.How came we by all that we think and know, or by all that we can think *?The answer to that question, if the right one, will show us where the mine of knowledge is, and how that mine can be worked ; and if we know these, no matter how small our present stock of knowledge may be, we shall soon and easily obtain more as much more as we please.That is a very simple question, a question the answer to which requires no philosophy, no learn- ing, no reading, nay not even the faculty of speech ; and yet that question is the seal upon all the possi- ble knowledge of which we are not in possession ; and many of us live long and go down to our graves in ignorance merely because we do not see, orj seeing, will not take the trouble to break that seal.That truth is so very important that we must dwell MERE SENSATION.the purely mental act of perceiving relation, and the mind's act through the senses in perceiving reality ; and for that reason we generally use only half our system work with half our strength.Not half of it even no, not a tenth ; for the real power is in the union of the two.When we use our senses, we do not think; and so the object of those senses can be turned to no profit, and give us no pleasure.If we do not think at the same time, the appearances of objects have no more effect upon our organs of sense than sun- beams when they play on the snow-clad summit of a lofty mountain ; they are reflected away in an in- stant ; and that which would have warmed a more genial place into life and beauty is gone wasted, never to return.How, scorpion-like, a little bit of the tail of some day spent in favourable places, but spent thoughtlessly, will turn and sting us with the remorse of how much we have lost, and lost never to be recalled or replaced !How often, even when the most delightfully instructive prospects are before us, have we reason to address ourselves in the words of Macbeth to the ghost of his murdered friend : " Thou hast no speculation in these eyes Which thou dost glare with."And we, too, are murderers, and murderers "red hand" in the fact, and not in the remorse caused by the dogging ghost of that which we are murdering.We are murdering Time the means of all know- ledge, and the measure of all enjoying ; and, inde- pendently of the direct loss, which is irreparable, if the ghost of murdered Time shall, at any period, rise and haunt us, it is one of the most terrible of ghosts, and we must abide its tormentings alone and unpitied.This abuse of our time, and neglect of thinking, instead of working its own cure, throws us into the opposite fault; and, just because we have gazed without thinking, we think without observing, andJose both the time and the thought ; and lose it in 'nature.If we loiter on the sleepless pillow, and have not resolution enough to get up, then our torment lasts till the dawn has so far advanced as that we can see distinctly, or till the beams of the early sun are breaking in through the chink of the shutters, or the opening of the curtains ; but soon after even the articles of the room are revealed to our observation, our minds are tranquillized, and we glide into dozing slumber.

venue: Journal of the Dermatology Nurses’ Association
abstract: The Dermatology Nurses' Association (DNA) reported in the 2021 Fourth Quarter FOCUS that the organization has 1,314 members (https://www.dnanurse.org/3d-flip-book/focus-fourth-quarter-2021/) (FOCUS: The Official Publication of the Dermatology Nurses' Association; Fourth Quarter 2021). I am thrilled to know there are over 1,300 dermatology nurses who are passionate about dermatology nursing as I am! I want to congratulate each of you who has taken the first step, becoming a DNA member and becoming part of the dermatology nursing community. The dermatology nursing community is passionate, diverse, engaging, and also welcoming to new nurses interested in the field. I have been a DNA member for 20 years and continue to be impressed with the quality and excellence the organization offers to its members. Aside from the Journal of the Dermatology Nurses' Association (JDNA), which I am obviously super proud of, the DNA has numerous opportunities and mechanisms to make dermatology nurses better educated and better equipped to address the complex healthcare needs of our patients, while acknowledging the current challenges of providing healthcare in the current system. How many of you participated in the recent DNA Annual Convention? The Convention agenda was available both as an in-person conference in Las Vegas, Nevada, and virtually for remote participation. And, wow, what great presentations there were. Annually, I typically share brief, bullet-point information from each Convention for those readers who were not able to participate. And this year is no different; but what is different this year is that there was so much pertinent, timely, accurate, and informative knowledge shared about a wide variety of dermatology topics, and I can only share some of this with you in this issue. I took over 20 pages of single-spaced notes! Hopefully you will enjoy the information shared here and tune in to the next issue to see the remainder of information. Here is just some of what was shared at the 40th Annual DNA Convention held in February 2022: Nurses are creative. We all have creative genius. Creative behavior can be learned and can be taught. You need to make time and space to nurture creativity. Gender nonconformity is not the same as gender dysphoria. The term transvestite is no longer used in the English language and is considered pejorative. Pemphigus and pemphigoid are blisters in mucous membranes and skin and are associated with mucosal erosions, blisters, and bumps. There are four types of pemphigus: pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus, IgA pemphigus, and paraneoplastic pemphigus. There are four types of pemphigoid: mucous membrane pemphigoid (cicatricial), bullous pemphigoid, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, and pemphigoid gestationis. Stress, physical trauma, sun exposure, and certain foods are all known to influence pemphigus and pemphigoid disease presentation and progression. Pemphigus and pemphigoid are not contagious and are not genetic. Rather, they are rare, autoimmune diseases for which long-term remission can be achieved. This disease can be fatal if left untreated. Treatment of pemphigus and pemphigoid consists of three phases: control, consolidation, and maintenance. However, relapse can occur at any time. Treatments for pemphigus can include oral and topical steroids, anti-inflammatory agents, immunosuppressants, biologics, and intravenous immunoglobulin. Good oral hygiene is important; patients should get regular dental cleanings. Blisters can form on the eyes. A patient may have dry eye symptoms. There can be a psychological burden to having a disease that is chronic, incurable, and unpredictable and a potentially embarrassing condition with a relapsing, remitting course. Anxiety, depression, and stress can be common. We need to spend time teaching patients. Teaching patients is an important role for dermatology nurses. It is important to use evidence-based therapy guidelines for atopic dermatitis. Terminology choice is important: eczema or dermatitis versus atopic dermatitis or atopic eczema. Use correct nomenclature when discussing with patients and family. There is a large differential diagnosis for atopic dermatitis. Atopic dermatitis is a clinical diagnosis. Biopsy may not be helpful. If the patient does not have itching, they likely do not have atopic dermatitis. Lichenification is common in chronic atopic dermatitis. The atopic triad consists of atopic dermatitis, asthma, and allergic rhinitis. Atopic dermatitis often affects quality of life. There is a complex pathophysiology of atopic dermatitis. These immune paths and activation of the immune system influence treatment options. Good basic skin care is essential in atopic dermatitis. Barrier repair remains a goal of atopic dermatitis management. Barrier repair reduces moisture loss that amplifies skin changes, strengthens the barrier function that protects against environmental triggers, maintains the stratum corneum acidity that protects against pathogens, and has a role in secondary prevention to help reduce recurrence of flares. If you do not like the people you work with, get a new job. Pearls for prescribing in atopic dermatitis: o Document the diagnosis of atopic dermatitis, not just eczema o Qualify and document severity of disease o Address prior therapies, therapeutic failures, and past treatments “Soak and Seal”—take a soaking bath in warm water daily, use gentle cleansers (fragrance free, dye free), pat away excess water, and immediately apply skin medications or moisturizer within 3 minutes. There is no clear frequency or duration for bathing. Gentle products and sensitive cleaning routines are important. Bleach baths continue to be controversial. Works well for patients with recurrent bacterial infections. However, these baths can be drying and irritating to the skin. Moisturizers daily are an important component of atopic dermatitis management. All moisturizers are not the same. Use one with a good track record. When looking at moisturizers, consider safety, active ingredients, side effects, vehicle, absorption, amount required, cost, cosmetic appeal, patient preference, and patient willingness to use. Good products to consider for atopic dermatitis include Aquaphor, Aveeno, CeraVe, Cetaphil, Eucerin Eczema Relief Formula, and Vanicream. How much product to use? To cover the average adult skin surface × 1 time, it takes 30 grams (1 oz). It takes 1 oz to cover the entire body. This is true for sunscreen, topical corticosteroids, and moisturizers. Be sure to recommend/prescribe the appropriate amount of medication. Give them enough medication to use the correct amount. Pruritus is the primary symptom of atopic dermatitis. How to treat itching? Considering using sedating or nonsedating antihistamines. Sedating antihistamines include diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, doxepin, and cetirizine. Yes, cetirizine is sedating—lower sedation, but still a sedating medication. Nonsedating antihistamines include desloratadine, loratadine, and fexofenadine. Keep fingernails clean, short, and smooth. Gloves are great options. The role of infection in atopic dermatitis cannot be overstated. Topical corticosteroids are the mainstay of anti-inflammatory therapy for atopic dermatitis in children and adults. There continues to be reluctance to use these medications, and patient education is essential. Topical calcineurin inhibitors include tacrolimus and pimecrolimus. These are nonsteroidal options, no skin atrophy is reported, and there is little systemic absorption. However, there is a black-box warning for this class of medication about the increased risk for malignancy, although there is no causal relationship established. Phosphodiesterase Type 4 inhibitor—approved in December 2016: crisaborole topical ointment 2%; nonsteroidal; this is not associated with atrophy, telangiectasias, or hypopigmentation. Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors—there are both topical and oral JAK inhibitors for atopic dermatitis; ruxolitinib cream 1.5% is a topical selective JAK inhibitor for mild-to-moderate atopic dermatitis. Oral JAK inhibitors have been approved for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. o Abrocitinib—an oral JAK inhibitor for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. Works by selectively blocking JAK1; dosing is available in once-daily oral tablets. o Upadacitinib—an oral JAK inhibitor approved for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis; available in once-daily, extended-release tablets. JAK inhibitors have a black-box warning for serious adverse events; must address their rationale for use with patients. Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended as a long-term treatment for atopic dermatitis. Biologic medications indicated for atopic dermatitis include dupilumab and tralokinumab-ldrm (Interleukin-13). Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is o a chronic, inflammatory, scarring condition; o affects intertriginous skin of axillary, inguinal, inframammary, genital, and perineal areas; and o causes recurrent inflamed deep-seated acneiform nodules that result in abscesses and chronic draining sinus tract formation leading to scarring. Primary lesions of HS are painful follicular papules or pustules, nodules, and abscesses. Secondary lesions include cysts, fistulas, double pseudocomedones, and scars. Diseases associated with HS include acne conglobata, dissecting cellulitis of the scalp, pilonidal cysts, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, and pyoderma gangrenosum. Comorbidities of HS can include obesity, acne, hyperlipidemia, depression, insulin resistance, pilonidal sinus, polycystic ovarian syndrome, diabetes, hypertension, and keratosis pilaris. Complications of HS can include fistulae into urethra, bladder, or rectum (rare); arthropathy; infections such as cellulitis, lumbosacral epidural abscess, and sacral bacterial osteomyelitis; lymphatic obstruction with lymphedema; complications from chronic inflammatory disease such as anemia, hypoproteinemia, and amyloidosis; squamous cell carcinoma; contractures and limb mobility limitations; and malaise, depression, suicide. Management of HS involves metabolic, medical, and surgical strategies. Treatment may include gentle local hygiene, diet to ideal weight, smoking cessation, topical and oral antibiotics, intralesional steroids, surgical therapy, immunosuppressive agents, oral retinoids, anti-inflammatory medications, and biologic medications, as well as use of hormonal treatments (spironolactone, finasteride), metformin, zinc, photodynamic therapy, botulinum toxin, x-ray radiation, cryosurgery, and laser treatments. Adalimumab is the only Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved biologic medication for HS. Practitioners may need a multidisciplinary team to treat patients with HS including dermatology, plastic surgery, rheumatology, gastroenterology, weight management, wound care, pain management, weight management/bariatric clinics, psychiatry/psychology, and smoking cessation clinics. Psoriasis types include plaque, scalp psoriasis, erythrodermic, nail psoriasis, and genital/inverse psoriasis. Efficacy of biologics js influenced by genetic variants such as disease susceptibility, drug response, and adverse drug reactions. Current therapies for psoriasis include topical therapies; narrow-band ultraviolet B; nonbiologic options such as methotrexate, cyclosporine, and acitretin as well as 11 FDA-approved biologics; and small-molecule inhibitor (apremilast). There is a difference between biologics (“mab” suffix) versus small molecules (“nib” or “tinib” suffix). Biologic medications—a protein; a living organism; fragile; the target is specific; given via injection or infusion; drug interactions often uncommon Biologic medications typically have a longer half-life. Small-molecule medications are manufactured, are not a living organism, are stable, and typically have daily dosing, usually oral. Biosimilars: FDA approved—etanercept (2), adalimumab (6), infliximab (4), and Phosphodiesterase Type 4 inhibitor (1); name includes generic plus a four-letter suffix. They are not automatically interchangeable. Be on the lookout for more information about this. There can be specific red flags to potentially emergent situations. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions include drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, necrotizing fasciitis, mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis, and erythema multiforme (EM). It is important to have recognition of urgent or emergent conditions. Red flag symptoms of dermatology include fever (and rash), age (very young or older adult), toxic-appearing/hypotension, immunocompromised, adenopathy, diffuse erythroderma, petechiae/purpura, recent new drug use within the last 1–4 weeks, arthralgias, mucous membrane involvement, and severe localized pain/tenderness in the extremity. Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms are often caused by antiepileptic drugs, sulfa-based medications, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, allopurinol, and abacavir. Facial edema is concerning with drug reactions. Necrotizing fasciitis is a bacterial infection that is a true surgical emergency. It is often found on the lower extremities but can occur anywhere. It can be staph, strep, MRSA, or polymicrobial, usually with a history of trauma (intravenous drug uses, skin popping); dusky or violaceous discoloration develops, which correlates with tissue death and necrosis, often resulting in significant pain. There may be a foul odor. For example, this could occur in someone with chronic tinea pedis. Pain that occurs is disproportionate to the erythema. Consult the surgeon very early if necrotizing fasciitis is in the differential. This condition can progress rapidly. Crepitus is air/gas in the tissue. If you palpate crepitus in the skin, this is an ominous sign. Mycoplasma-induced rash and mucositis—prominent mucous membrane involvement; common in children; usually mild course; there will not be progression to toxic epidermal necrolysis. EM—a viral infection with two variations: o EM minor—can be drug related, usually postviral; will see three ring target lesions, usually acral (palms, soles), no mucous membrane involvement, not ill appearing o EM major—can have mucosal involvement; systemic symptoms will be present; cutaneous lesions—targetoid, atypical targets, blisters, central and not widespread. Not all mucous membrane involvement is Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Fatigue + fever + rash = red flag! Lyme disease, if untreated, can lead to heart block and sudden cardiac death. Bell's palsy can be seen with Lyme disease. Meningococcal meningitis: be concerned for this if there is a history of upper respiratory infection, especially in younger children or those in communal living. Meningococcal meningitis is transmitted through respiratory droplets. Always consider meningococcal meningitis in the differential diagnosis in children with high fever, progressive petechial eruption and hypotension, purpura, and flu-like symptoms. It is meningococcal meningitis until proven otherwise. Nuchal rigidity is not always present in the presentation of meningococcal meningitis. Common symptoms of meningococcal disease include cold hands and feet, hemorrhagic rash, and photophobia. These will vary based on age demographic. Call 911 if this patient is sitting in your dermatology office with these symptoms. title: Incilius spiculatus
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Results Tadpole Description Average measurements (mm) for Gosner stage 35: body length 13.28, tail length 21.68, tail muscle height 3.41, maximum tail height 6.09, total length 34.96, tail muscle width 3.31, internarial distance 1.66, interorbital distance 4.70; measurements for other Gosner stages are presented in Table 1. The body is ovoid in dorsal view, widest at about the middle point and narrower near the tail; depressed in lateral view. Snout nearly semicircular in dorsal profile, rounded at the tip in lateral profile. Spiracle sinistral with inner wall free from body. External nares ovoid situated nearer to eyes than to snout. Eyes dorsal. Vent tube medial. Tail rounded at the tip. Caudal musculature highest at base, gradually tapering to a pointed tip; dorsal fin reticulated (Fig. 1). Oral disk small; labial tooth row formula 2(2)/3, A1 slightly longer than other rows; A2 gap narrow, approximately width of 3–8 teeth, P1 and P2 equal in length, P3 being the longest posterior row; labial papillae restricted to lateral portions of oral disc disposed in two interposed series (Fig. 1A). At stage 24, the larvae show an elongation of the oral apparatus that protrudes from the body (Fig. 2D–E). In life, the color of the body is uniformly Cinnamon Brown (color 43 in Köhler 2012), except for the ventral part of the mouth where the color becomes paler. The venter is slightly transparent, with a counter-clockwise coiled intestine visible. Around Gosner stage 35, small Cream Yellow (82) dots appear throughout the body and the iris (Fig. 2G). The tail fins are transparent with large Cinnamon Brown (43) pigment granules forming a reticulate pattern on the dorsal fin. Around Gosner stage 37, the ventral parts of the limbs are pale Cinnamon Brown (43) with Cream Yellow (82) dots and dark brown bars dorsally. In preservative, the tadpole body and the tail musculature are Natal Brown (49), while the ventral part of the body is slightly translucent. Tadpole development required approximately 35 days to complete metamorphosis under laboratory conditions (Fig. 2H). Three days after collection (8 February 2019), embryonic development reached Gosner stage 12. Three days later, the embryos had reached stage 18, and four days after that had developed into stage 25 tadpoles. Adult Breeding Behavior In February 2019, an amplecting pair of Incilius spiculatus was observed at 640 m asl in the shallower margins of a river (Río Coyul), where the water current was slowed by the presence of rocks and aquatic vegetation. The Río Coyul is a permanent river with an average width of 8.19 m at the site where the amplexus was observed (Fig. 2F). The toads used vegetation and material on the bottom of the river to maintain their position in the water during the amplexus. Mating was observed during the day and the amplexus was axillary (Fig. 2A–B). At the time of the observations (1250 h GST), the water temperature was 19.6 °C. The species exhibited an ovipositional string mode with a double row of eggs arrangement (Altig and McDiarmid 2007). The estimated clutch size was 4,500 eggs, and the clutch was attached to aquatic vegetation on rocks at the river margins at about 35 cm depth (Fig. 2C). Amplectant behavior was observed from the time of encounter until the toads separated (approximately 2.67 h). The female body temperature was 21.0 °C, SVL 85.5 mm, and the clutch temperature was 21.0 °C. In addition to the amplectant pair, a second male toad was observed in the water at a distance of 1.0 m. A second egg clutch was observed in another pool located 3.70 m away; but the toads that laid this clutch were not observed. Adult Diet Fecal samples indicated that Hymenoptera were the dominant prey (15 individuals, 48.3%), followed by Coleoptera (7, 22.5%), Scorpiones (6, 19.3%), Orthoptera (2, 6.4%), and Blattodea (1, 3.2%). Extension of Elevational Range Previously, the elevational range reported for I. spiculatus was from 800–1,689 m asl (Mendelson 1997). During this survey, two juvenile individuals were observed at Santa Cruz Tepetotutla, Oaxaca, Mexico, in a patch of primary cloud forest vegetation at an elevation of 1,758 m asl (17.71862°N, - 96.55911°W) datum WGS84, in addition to three individuals in San Pedro Yolox at 682 m asl (17.63622°N, - 96.42735°W), 643 m asl (17.64001 °N, - 96.43061°W), and 642 m asl (17.64013°N, - 96.43056°W). With these records, the altitudinal range of this species is now extended as including from 642 to 1,758 m asl. Key to the tadpoles of the forest toads of Mexico and Central America 1a.
