Accessed May 2009 Google Scholar 2 National Center for Complementary and Alternative Medicine (2009) NCCAM Grand Opportunities (“GO”) Grants. http://nccam.nih.gov/recovery/go.htm Google Scholar 3Weissmann, G. (2007) Galileo's Gout. Bellevue Literary Press, New York. p. 118– 123 Google Scholar Volume23, Issue8August 2009Pages 2337-2340 ReferencesRelatedInformation

title: Strata
abstract: My husband and I had found the desert house accidentally. Each winter, we'd leave our snowy northern home for a few weeks and head to Death Valley to join other pale snowbirds on a heat-seeking mission. We checked out of our overly busy lives to wander mosaic canyons and moonlit dunes. We said hello to lizards and stretched our winter-tight bodies. We took pictures of each other waist high in leggy golden desert daisies; it was a delight to see my burly blond husband frolic in wildflowers. Because of his work, I rarely see him; these photos are proof of life.The year my mother had her “gather the family” stroke, which she partially survived—her mind did not—we ventured farther south, to Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, California's largest at 600,000 acres. A tiny town that would not look out of place in Mexico sits in the middle of it. The houses were cheap and the weather fine. Thinking it would be a place we went for respite during our working years, and, for me, from caregiving, we staked a claim. It was a retreat, we agreed, so far from civilization that we might never be found.For three years, I managed the care of my dying parents. My life was triangle-shaped: from our primary home to their apartment and to the desert, where my husband would sometimes join me. When my parents died, one corner of the triangle fell off; what remained pointed to the desert house. I packed their ashes into a beautifully appointed rice container that my sister in Thailand had given us for our wedding. “It's only temporary,” I told them. Then I put my parents in the van and headed south.The desert house is on a half acre and is surrounded by a stucco half wall, which the neighbors refer to as a “moat.” I like the moat. It keeps out coyotes and the trash that sometimes breaks loose in epic windstorms. The moat feels like a layer of protection I need right now. It feels like a safe place to mourn.The yard has a succulent and cactus garden filled with showcase specimens of Engelmann's prickly pear and paddle cactus. I sit with coffee and watch hummingbirds dip into the chuparosa and drink. White-winged doves coo in stereo. Ravens alight the California fan palms at high noon, tormenting our old border collie, Angus, whose job is to guard everything inside the moat. Jackrabbits have found refuge from coyotes here, and roadrunners cruise the back deck. When the roadrunners arrive, I know the snakes are on their way.The yard has five citrus trees, so I've become an accidental farmer, learning about soil and the trickiness of growing limes, but not lemons, which give and give. With so many lemons, I think there is a still a chance for a lemonade life.Anza-Borrego is wow country. No matter which way you enter, from the Salton Sea through the Borrego Badlands, dropping through the layers of rock on Montezuma Pass, or via the Texas Dip, you say “Wow.” You wonder what the hell happened to make it look like this. You feel like you're driving across another planet.I have fallen hard for this place. The blaze and tangle of rocky canyons, the palm oases, the precise elemental balance. The story of the universe laid out in stone. I want to understand this particular mayhem of granite and iron and star. The strata—the layers of how a place came to be—look like tiramisu.This desert, the Colorado Desert, a claw-shaped piece of the vast Sonoran, seems big enough to hold my grief.My mom had vascular dementia, and was in a nursing home during the pandemic when she died. We'd kept her at home as long as we could, until she started trying to escape, not understanding there was no way out of her own ragged mind. She passed at ninety-one years old without family in a sterile room and with little touch the last few months of her life. This was a woman who worked as a professional clown and wore a “Free Hugs” button on her shirt. My mom loved people and in the end she had none. I hope her inaccurate but happy memories gave her comfort.The last time I saw her, we did a window visit because of COVID. It was a perfect day in Napa. Grape vines and sunshine. The nursing staff, outfitted like astronauts, rolled her up to the window in an empty room. She was on a special mattress, big and black and puffy, so she wouldn't get bedsores. Contractures were settling in at her joints and she was folding in on herself. On that big dark mattress, she looked like a nautilus spinning in space.Over the course of a forty-minute visit, she never opened her eyes. I sat outside the window and whispered that she'd been a good mom and that I loved her and that I'd never forget spaghetti Sundays or watching old movies together. I talked to her until I ran out of things to say. I convinced myself that she looked peaceful, and then I drove away. Eventually, she stopped eating, which is common in dementia, but she kept taking her medication with a protein drink that kept her alive until finally it didn't. She died early one morning after my visit. Her hospice nurse told me the Buddhists believe it's auspicious to take flight in the morning.Six months before, I had moved in with my dad, who had congestive heart failure. He lived a half hour from the nursing home, so that drive became my groove. I had promised him that when he started hospice, I would return to my hometown and stay with him until the end. I kept COVID at bay, masking up to shop at 6 a.m. I couldn't keep him from the news, though. I tried to reassure him that I would survive the virus and the assaults of the current federal administration, and I hope he believed me when he finally let go. I'm making it sound gentle because I was there, his hand in mine as his last heartbeat circled, and he did not struggle for air. Still, I didn't know that a broken heart could break any further until mine broke again. He left in the morning, too.Back at home, I received a package in the mail. Who sent me a gift? I wondered. Inside was my dad, double-bagged. A few weeks passed and I got a second, smaller box. This time I knew what it was. I relocated their ashes to the rice container. I took them to the desert with me because I didn't want them to get cold.We arrive at the dead end at Green Links Drive, Angus and I. It's 8:08 a.m. Our daily walk in Borrego is like going to a bar. We can always count on the regulars. It's early morning and the bunnies and quails are here. The innocents, each with a comical head topping that is convenient for predators to spot. The jackrabbits with those long ears; when the sun shines through you can see the lacy circuitry of blood. And the quails, with a fancy comma on top, bustle as if they are late for the bus.If we come at 8:30, the young, lean coyotes are out on play dates. The humans follow: the overly tan, thin woman who looks like a strip of bacon and always waves; the man with the fancy dog who doesn't smile. The jogger who pitches forward as he runs, so much that I worry for him.There are ducks at the watering hole, an aesthetic at this fallowed golf course that the landowners keep filled for the animals. The Canada geese return and the vultures sun themselves and wait. Same as it ever was.I feel right-sized here. The 8 a.m. woman with dog passing through. No more important than the shapely mesquite trees that house creatures and provide food and shade. Maybe even less so. Maybe the mesquite tree is more important than me, from the species that takes and takes. I wonder if it's possible for me to be as useful and lovely as a mesquite tree. That seems like a worthy goal. I file it to consider, on the other side of grief.My husband works in education, and has arrived for Christmas break. I knew when I married him sixteen years before that I would come second to his vocation, which is fighting for teachers. Union work puts a fire in his belly, and gives him purpose. His phone is an extension of his hand, and he's usually negotiating or bargaining or talking someone down. I understand wanting to be needed. But I need him too; I'm lonely inside the moat. We will have two weeks together, which seems like a feast.Even so, he spends most of his time working. I tell myself it's fine, at least he's nearby. We have coffee together in the morning and dinner at night; every now and then I can talk him into a Jeep ride or a little hike. I don't notice that I'm still mostly alone. His busyness fills the days like clouds.He's at the computer when I tell him I'm going for a hike and I'll be back in an hour. He looks at me over the top of his glasses and waves. Thirty minutes into the trail I round the corner in one of my favorite ocotillo forests. The late afternoon light casts them in a lush blue-green. I see a herd of five large and muscular bighorn rams, grinding their way through grass and cacti. They lift their enormous horns and consider me with widely spaced eyes. They determine I am not a threat and resume grazing. Some eventually move on, leaping to new boulders with delicate grace. There are likely ewes and babies nearby, maybe an errant teenager testing the waters. I know I will not be home in an hour, whatever that is. I'm on bighorn time.A friend recently wrote in a letter, “It must be wonderful waking up in wild open land.”It feels like a return to life.In the picture, I am not yet two years old. It's sepia-toned and I'm in the pine trees. I am striding alone through the forest wearing a smile in half shadow. I'm dressed in a baby jumper and sandals. My legs are strong and I walk with purpose. Do we each have a picture like this, captured of our most essential selves—the marine layer or magma—the person the world will try to destroy? I feel her trying to emerge here from the brutality of grief. Plates are shifting.My husband tries to stay with us in our desert home, but the pandemic has unmoored him. He feels too far away from his colleagues, even though he sees them on Zoom every day. He returns to the north, a snowbird in reverse. You're going in the wrong direction, I think. Just look at the Western bluebirds, they know. I let him go because I want him to be happy.In his absence, I seek comfort in rocks and their stories. I become obsessed with the geologic time scale. Growing up, I had childhood asthma and missed a lot of school—it turns out I had missed the dinosaur lessons. I started asking friends when they first learned about dinosaurs or had dinosaur curriculum.“Second grade?” one said. “I feel like I was always learning about dinosaurs,” said another. I had some catching up to do. I bought a poster, and like a middle-school science teacher I tacked it to the wall in the guest bedroom, determined to learn the eras and periods.I grow my desert library. I pack a milk crate of reference books everywhere I go because there is so much to learn. Every hole in my yard is the entrance to someone's home. There is an entire network of subterranean life under my feet. The subway of the cold blooded, passing each other by. I think of those cross sectional images from biology class and that I've got millions and millions of years to dissect. This keeps me busy.Given that he is working exclusively online, my husband doesn't have many reasons to stay away, yet he does. “I'm waiting for my vaccine,” he says.The girl in the woods in the sepia photo keeps walking in half-shadow, doing what she is built to do: Look, listen.My mom and dad's marriage formed a layer of my personal strata when their families drifted from Europe to Appalachia to the San Francisco Bay Area, where they lived on opposite sides of a steel-span bridge. They met at a Mexican bar and restaurant, where my mom liked to dance.In a flush of hormones I was made. They were, however, ill-suited for each other, incongruent, like sandstone and marble side-by-side in a dry wash. The forces of poverty and stubbornness were the erosions that wore them down, but by some miracle, maybe California sunshine, they stayed together for over fifty years. Mom was a real razzmatazz, an entertainer who loved being in the middle of the action. She was a woman in motion, who would sometimes get out of a car before it stopped moving. Like my husband, she was rarely home, preferring being needed at work to domestic life. Dad was a man of few words who spent his spare time at a fishing hole. They had separate bedrooms, took separate vacations. Family was the glue that kept them together, like desert concrete, made when wind blows on rocks and earth so hard and long they bind together.Dad's hospice nurse showed up every day in good cheer, bringing calm and a full quiver of palliative skills. First she tended to his immediate physiological needs, and next she listened to his fears. Then she'd sit with me in the living room and listen to mine.I talked to her about my dad's imminent death, and how to keep him comfortable. About the rift my mom's dementia created between them, before her safety made us place her in a nursing home.I tell the nurse I'm missing my own husband. I want to take a weekend and go home. She asks me if I'd be okay with my dad dying while I was gone. Although the nurse never talks in absolutes, I understand this shorthand.We were sitting on the couch, our knees so close they almost touched. The nurse asked me about my marriage, how we're holding up. I told her we're fine, that my husband has his own life. “We either relive our parents’ marriage or we reinvent it,” she said, and I grabbed onto her words like a rope. I wondered if we could reinvent ours. title: 2018 Academy Proceedings
venue: Journal of North Carolina Academy of Science
abstract: The one hundredth and fifteenth annual meeting of the North Carolina Academy of Science, Inc. was held at Wake Technical Community College located in Raleigh, North Carolina, March 23 and 24 of 2018 with the Collegiate Academy (CANCAS) joining the Senior Academy. The conference theme was Collaborate, Communicate, Contribute—Connecting Scientists with the Public.Activities Friday, March 23, took place at Wake Technical Community College's Southern Wake Campus. The meeting began with the Finance and Strategic Planning Committee meeting at 1:00 p.m. followed by a Senior Academy meeting of the Board of Directors from 2:00–5:00 p.m. in the SM 343 & 345 conference rooms. Registration for the Academy Annual Meeting ran from 5:00–6:00 p.m. in the lobby of Building L. The poster session was held in the main room of Building L and the conference reception in the pre-function area with food provided for guests and presenters from 6:00–7:30 p.m. There were fifty-four posters representing research in the areas of Botany, Ecology, & Environmental Sciences; Cell & Development, Molecular Biology; Chemistry, Engineering & Physics, Science Education; Genetics, Physiology; and Microbiology. Students were present to answer questions and discuss their findings throughout the evening. Judges for the CANCAS posters met prior to the session and after the session. The poster session was followed by opening and welcoming remarks in the lobby. Welcome remarks were given by Dr. Brandie Littlefield and Dr. Scott Johnson, Wake Technical Community College, Co-chairs of the Local Arrangements Committee, and Dr. Alan Goble, President of NCAS. President Goble then dedicated the 2018 NCAS annual meeting to Dr. John Clamp (1949–2018). Dr. Clamp was a longtime, deeply involved member of the Academy from his undergraduate years at Methodist University and throughout his tenure as a faculty member at NC Central University.On Saturday, March 24, activities were held in Building L, SC 105A, and SC 105B. Registration was held in Building L Lobby from 7:30–8:15 a.m. Exhibits and tables of vendors, meeting sponsors, and the graduate school fair, which provided information about several graduate programs in North Carolina, were available in Building L from 8:30 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. There were twenty-two Collegiate Academy oral presentations given in three morning sessions, 8:30–9:30 a.m.; 9:45–10:30 a.m.; and 11:00–11:45 a.m. Oral session one consisted of three concurrent groups: Biotechnology & Molecular Biology; Environmental Sciences; and Microbiology, for a total of ten presentations. Oral session two consisted of three concurrent groups: Microbiology; Chemistry & Physiology; and Genomics & Physiology, for a total of nine presentations. Oral session three consisted of Faculty & Graduate Student Presentations, for a total of three presentations. Seven poster presentations by high school students, members of the Student Academy, were on display with presenters standing by their posters from 9:30 a.m. to 10:00 a.m.From 11:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. two workshops were offered, one focusing on finding careers and the second on conducting research at community colleges. “Workshop one: Alternative Careers to Academia” featured five panelists discussing their unique career paths; the panelists were: Richard Bergl, Ph.D., Director of Conservation, Education, and Science Department at the North Carolina Zoo; Jim Connor, environmental lawyer and Partner at Calhoun, Bhella, Sechrest; David M. DeMarini, Ph.D., Genetic Toxicologist at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; Rebecca Guenard, Ph.D., Science Reporter; and Julie Horvath, Ph.D., Head of the Genomics & Microbiology Research Lab, NC Museum of Natural Sciences. “Workshop two: Research at Community Colleges” featured four panelists discussing the importance and challenges in conducting research at community colleges; the panelists were: David Beamer, Instructor, Biology, Nash Community College; Ashley Hagler, M.S., M.A.T., Gaston College; Scott Nunez, Ph.D., Instructor, Biology, Wake Technical Community College; and Rachel Walsh, Ph.D., Instructor, Biology, Wake Technical Community College. All workshops were interesting and incredibly informative to attendees.At the conclusion of morning presentations and workshops, lunch was served to meeting registrants in the pre-function area of Building L from 12:00–1:15 p.m., concurrently a meeting was held of judges to determine CANCAS Derieux awards for the morning presentations.Remarks and the keynote address were held from 1:15–2:45 p.m. in Building L. The Keynote Speaker, Michael A. Palladino, Ph.D., Vice Provost for Graduate Studies, Professor of Biology from Monmouth University in West Long Branch, New Jersey inspired and engaged the audience with his interactive and humorous presentation on communicating science and making it accessible for everyone.Following a coffee break from 2:45 to 3:00 p.m. the Senior Academy Annual Business Meeting & Board of Directors Meeting and the Collegiate Academy (CANCAS) Business Meeting ran concurrently from 3:00–4:00 p.m. The Senior Academy met in SC 105A and CANCAS met in SC 105B. From 4:00–4:45 p.m. meeting attendees were treated to a reception and awards ceremony in Building L.The two-day annual meeting was attended by 272 people.President Alan Goble called the meeting to order at 3:04 p.m. with twenty-four people in attendance.The minutes of the 2017 Business meeting were presented and approved.Francie Cuffney, head of the nominating committee, presented the slate of officers for 2018–2019:A motion was made to vote for the slate by acclimation. The motion was seconded and the slate of officers was passed by acclimation.Slate of non-elected positions include:Reports:President: Dr. Alan GobleSecretary: Dr. Maria PickeringThe Board of Directors met four times over the past year (i.e., May, Sept 2017 and Jan and March 23, 2018) since the last annual business meeting. September and March were in-person meetings here at Wake Tech and 2 were virtual meetings using Blackboard Collaborate in (May and January); the Board will continue to alternate in-person and virtual meetings in the coming year.Approximately 326 people attended last year's annual meeting held at High Point University located in High Point, North Carolina, March 24 and 25 of 2017. Fifty percent were undergraduates.In May, the Board discussed Board responsibilities and went over NCAS mission and goals. Membership, the Annual Meeting, and Outreach were focus topics for the 2017–2018 year.In January, NCAS had a successful educational booth at the NC Museum of Natural Sciences Astronomy Days entitled “The Quest for Extraterrestrial Life,” highlighting organisms on Earth that live in extreme habitats.The journal is published electronically and access for members is in the process of being resolved. All members are encouraged to submit articles and become reviewers, and encourage your colleagues as well.The Board of Directors examined the NCAS By-Laws and voted to make 2 changes: Changes to the By-Laws: removed 3 membership categories and created a new article called Sponsorships (Sustaining, Associate, and Institutional), which better reflects what they are, and that requires the renumbering of articles accordingly. Under membership year we changed it to reflect that it now runs from annual meeting to annual meeting (versus the calendar year).Finally, the Board has developed a Temporary Action Group (TAG) that will meet in the coming months and focus on improving and strengthening the Academy's online presence moving forward.Finance Committee: Dr. Eid HaddadTreasurer: Dr. Shana McAlexanderTreasurer's Report—Shana McAlexanderCurrent bank balances and total net worth (not including NCSAS):Shana McAlexander distributed copies of the proposed budget for 2019.Proposed 2019 Annual BudgetThe 2019 budget was approved unanimously.Journal Editor: Dr. Mark McCallumDr. Mark McCallum is the Managing Editor (contact about publications). Please encourage colleagues to submit; there are short communications available for undergraduate projects. Since the journal is a continuous publication there is a quicker turn-around time. If any students submit, they get the first three pages free.Resolution of ThanksResolution of Thanks for Wake Technical Community College (Resolutions for 115th Annual Meeting of the North Carolina Academy of Science at Wake Technical Community College, Raleigh, NC) – Dr. Judy Moore. Resolution passed by acclimation:“Whereas the 2018 Annual Meeting of the North Carolina Academy of Science at Wake Technical Community College in Raleigh, North Carolina, has been dedicated with deep respect to Dr. John Clamp (1949–2018). John was a longtime, deeply involved member of the Academy beginning in his undergraduate years at Methodist University and continuing through his graduate studies and throughout his tenure as a faculty member at NC Central University. He was a member of the Board of Directors beginning as an elected member in 2001, served a term as president (2003–2004), chaired the membership committee from 2004 until 2010, and was a most knowledgeable parliamentarian from 2009 until his passing. His institutional memories helped us maintain continuity as NCAS moved forward. He was most proud of the privilege he had to educate, mentor, and inspiring countless students and researchers. John was a lover of the outdoors, an avid fisherman, hiker, gardener and birdwatcher. He is remembered fondly by this Academy.Whereas the 2018 Annual Meeting of the North Carolina Academy of Science at Wake Technical Community College, the first time a community college has ever hosted the event, has been a great success;Whereas the members of the Academy and other attendees appreciated and were inspired by the ingenuity and industry of senior members and students conducting scientific investigations, summarized in their oral and poster presentations. Additionally, there were opportunities throughout the meeting for social interactions, networking, and enjoyment of good food and refreshments;Whereas Dr. Michael Paladino inspired us with his keynote address that emphasized this meeting's theme “Collaborate-Communicate-Contribute” by elaborating on the important role of scientists as public advocates for science and sharing specific ways we can be involved.Whereas two career workshops were offered to highlight alternative careers to academia and research at community colleges, both conducted by knowledgeable and informative panelists; thereforeBe it resolved that the North Carolina Academy of Science expresses its appreciation for the huge efforts of the Local Arrangements Committee for planning, organizing, stewarding and working with Wake Technical Community College for a successful and energizing annual meeting, chaired by Dr. Brandie Littlefield and Dr. Scott Johnson,Be it resolved that the North Carolina Academy of Science expresses its deepest gratitude and appreciation for the hospitality of Wake Technical Community College, including Dr. Stephen C. Scott President, the Wake Tech Department of Mathematics, Science and Engineering, and the faculty, staff and students of Wake Technical Community College.”Presentation of CertificatesPresident Alan Goble announced members of the Board who are either stepping down or completing a term of office and who will receive certificates of appreciation:Plaque of AppreciationDr. Alan Goble announced the transfer of presidency to Dr. Jean-Luc Scemama. A plaque of appreciation was presented to Immediate Past President Dr. Alan Goble.Request from President Jean-Luc Scemama: nominate someone for President-Elect and send to him in the next 2 weeks; if do not want to be president consider joining a committee.The meeting adjourned at 3:48 P.M.New CANCAS Officers and Campus Liaisons (2018–2019)Campus Liaisons:Charles Bookheimer (bookheimercm@guilford.edu); Guilford CollegeTrina Phan (trinapphan@gmail.com); North Carolina StateKyle Weidner (weidnerk16@students.ecu.edu); East Carolina UniversityBeverly Anaele (ba233631@my.ncwc.edu); NC Wesleyan UniversityHenri Vega-Bernal (hvegabernal334@st.nashcc.edu); Nash Community CollegeOsvaldo Rodriguez (oarodriguez@my.waketech.edu); Wake Technical Community CollegeHana Rutland (hana.rutland@my.lr.edu); Lenoir Rhyne UniversityMicaela Robson (mjrobson0828@email.campbell.edu); Campbell UniversityNew Co-DirectorCANCAS welcomes Dr. Laura Reichenberg (Pfeiffer University) as a new co-director. Dr. Reichenberg will join Dr. Daniel Stovall (NC Wesleyan University) as co-director. We also thank Dr. Beth Cauley for all of her dedication, service, and leadership in CANCAS over the past four years!CANCAS continues to recruit student campus liaisons from CANCAS member institutions; if interested, contact Dr. Dan Stovall (dstovall@ncwc.edu). NC Wesleyan College has agreed to host the CANCAS Fall Workshop on Saturday, November 3. If you would like to be involved in running an interactive and engaging workshop for undergraduates, please contact either Daniel Stovall (dstovall@ncwc.edu) or Laura Reichenberg (laura.reichenberg@pfeiffer.edu).Students from across the state attended the CANCAS Annual Undergraduate Research Workshop on Saturday, November 4, 2017 at Campbell University. Our workshop was held in conjunction with SNCURCS, and it was a great success! In addition to hearing about exciting undergraduate research through SNCURCS presentations, approximately 80 CANCAS students got to tour Campbell University's School of Osteopathic Medicine & other health science programs. Another 50 CANCAS attendees also participated in various workshops.Justin Perkins, an English major at Campbell University and career services intern, helped students assess their unique experiences to examine how they are developing top employer-sought skills. Betsy Dunn-Williams, Director of Academic Support and Career Development at Campbell, led a workshop in which attendees learned how to build a professional social media presence and utilize best practices in resume and CV development. Dr. Karen Guzman, Professor of Biology at Campbell University, headed up a session on how to communicate effectively in oral and poster presentations – critical skills for any budding scientist. Kayla Taylor, Director of the Career & Professional Development Center at Campbell's law school, taught students how to design a meaningful work statement and navigate the pursuit of a purposeful career. Finally, Dr. Michele Malotky, Professor of Biology at Guilford College, presented students with opportunities for study abroad and the impact they can have on a college experience.CANCAS is grateful to Campbell University for hosting our fall workshop series, and to SNCURCS for their willingness to partner for these events!Bryden Graduate GrantsCongratulations to our two 2017–2018 Bryden Graduate Grant winners! title: History of venereal and skin diseases in Egypt from 1825 to 1924, AD
venue: Egyptian Journal of Dermatology and Venerology
abstract: At the end of the 18th century, there was no medical education or medical training in Egypt like the medical education available in many European countries. We hereby shed light on the development of the specialty of Dermatology and Venereology in Egypt and the evolution of Al-Qasr al-Aini from 1825–1924 AD. At the end of the 18th century, there was no medical education or medical training in Egypt like the medical education available in many European countries e.g., France, Austria, etc. [1]. On June 1, 1798, the French military leader Napoleon Bonaparte, accompanied by a few soldiers invaded Egypt. His troops were accompanied also by 150 scholars in all branches of science and art. In 1799, he established a field hospital for his military forces in the Qasr al-Aini area (Manial). In October 1801, Napoleon’s military campaign lefted Egypt after the Egyptian resistance. Despite its short duration, this military campaign had some positives, as it awakened the Egyptians to the reality of their backwardness Mohammed Ali arrived in 1801 to oust the French from Egypt. By 1805, M. Ali (1769–1849) was named the Wali (ruler), the Ottoman Sultan’s viceroy in Egypt, with the rank of ‘Pasha’. M. Ali seized the governorship for four decades. Afterwards, Mohammed Ali troops suffered during his military campaigns in Sudan in 1820–1821 due to infections and diseases that killed his soldiers more than the battles [2]. M. Ali realized the necessity of having a medical corps accompanying his military forces, in terms of military doctors and pharmacists [3]. In 1825, based on the recommendation of the French consul in Egypt, M. Ali invited Dr. Antoine Clot and 20 French doctors to come to Egypt to establish a medical school like those hospitals in France. M. Ali appointed Dr. Clot in 1825 as the chief army physician, and his title was ‘Hakimbashi Al-Jihadiya’ [4]. When Dr. Clot arrived in Egypt in 1825, only 50 European physicians and pharmacists were attached to the 150000-man army. Dr. Clot advised M. Ali about the necessity of introducing the rules followed in the French army to the Egyptian army, the necessity of sending medical missions from the Egyptian students to France, and the necessity of Arabizing medicine and translating of medical books [5]. In 1827, M. Ali built a huge medical edifice in ‘Abu Zaabal’ desert, to be a medical center that included a school and a hospital to serve the nearby ‘Jihad Abad’ camp. Against formidable odds, Dr Clot succeeded in launching Egypt’s first western school of medicine [6]. In November 1832, the first integrated medical delegation consisting of 12 students arrived in France with Dr. Clot. Its members were elected from the students at the medical school in Abu Zaabal. They were examined by the French Medical Association and achieved remarkable success [7]. One of the most famous members of this mission was Dr. Muhammad Al-Baqli. He became head of the medical school in Qasr El Aini from 1863 to 1876 when he was martyred in the Ethiopian War. Dr. Al-Baqli wrote a treatise on purulent conjunctivitis to obtain his baccalaureate degree [8]. A treatise in medicine was among the requirements to obtain a degree in medicine and surgery (baccalaureate) in the French medical school. During the first ten years of the establishment of the medical school, about 420 doctors were graduated to serve in the army [9]. After the significant reduction in the strength of the Egyptian army early in the 1840s, Qasr al-Aini was transformed into a multi-specialty medical center, and its impact extended to aspects of society that went beyond mere army service. Hundreds of doctors were appointed to jobs throughout the country in the ‘health offices‘ which provided free medical care to the poor and needy. The preserved records show the prevailing reasons for people’s dealings with hospitals and health offices that were established in the cities. In most cases, people resorted to hospitals due to very serious diseases, and syphilis was the main disease mentioned, whether for men, women, or prisoners [10]. It must be remembered that the purpose of establishing the entire medical institution was to serve the army. A nursing school was established in 1832 and a school for midwives was established in 1837 in the Qasr Al-Aini area. All men and women were subjected to strict military discipline and had military ranks. Patients were also subject to strict military discipline. A rare description in one of the writings of the French writer ‘Gustave Flaubert’ [11] who visited the ‘Syphilis’ ward in Qasr Al-Aini in the year 1849; ‘Qasr Al-Aini’ hospital is in excellent condition, the achievement of Clot Bey − his hand can still see beautiful cases of syphilis. Many were infected with it in their buttocks and when a signal comes from the doctor, they all stand on their beds and open their anuses with their fingers, revealing their genital ulcers, and huge cavities [12]. In 1861, (Godard) a French doctor described Al-Qasr Al-Aini as the only hospital in Cairo. He described the women’s ward, which was divided into three wards [13]: (a) Surgery ward, capacity for 47 patients. (b) Franchise diseases (venereal) ward, capacity for 26 patients. (c) Internal diseases ward, capacity for 15 patients. At the beginning of the 19th century, the population of Egypt was estimated to be about 2.5 million people and became 6.5 million by the end of the same century. A growing number of European residents in Egypt, estimated to be 5000 foreigners in 1840. Influx continued to 68000 by 1878. The number continued to grow due to the prosperity and peace in Egypt during the 1st and 2nd world wars with the influx of a huge number of immigrants, refugees, prostitutes, etc. during the first half of the 20th century. Four medical topics were the main concern of the work of the medical establishment throughout the country and ports [14]: (a) Hospitals. (b) Quarantine (Karantina). (c) Vaccination against smallpox. (d) Medical examination and body autopsies. Rare statistics indicate the extent of some diseases in Cairo (Tables 1 and 2) showing that venereal diseases were a common ailment at that time. Table 1 - Diseases prevalent in municipal outpatient clinics in Cairo from 1845 to 1847 Number Diseases 198 Emergency 327 Scorpion sting 456 Infectious diseases 534 Trauma 607 Smallpox 766 Scabies 958 Venereal diseases 1227 Internal ailments 3111 Fractures Table 2 - Classification of cases treated in Kasr Al-Aini Military Hospital from 1847 to 1848 [15] Number of Deaths Discharged Number of Cases Diagnosis 357 5592 5949 Internal Ailments – 1846 1846 Eye diseases 37 2350 2387 Surgery – 5136 5136 Venereal diseases 394 14924 15318 Total Herein a review of some of the venereologists and dermatologists whose names were mentioned in the 19th and first quarter of the 20th century: (1) Mustafa Al-Waty Bey. (2) Abd al-Rahman al-Hawari Bey. (3) Hassan Mahmoud Shaltut Pasha. (4) Mohammad Salem Bey. (5) Mohammad Radouan Effindi. (6) Prof. Dr Portocalis. (7) Dr. Fakhry Mikhaïl Farag. Mustafa Al-Waty Bey (Died 1864) Born in Al-Wat village, Menouf District, Menoufia. In the year 1842, he was the head of one of the translation departments, established by M. Ali Pasha under the supervision of Rifa’a Bey Al-Tahtawi. Al-Tahtawi sent M. Al-Waty to study medicine in France in 1845 for two years, then he completed his studies at the Al-Qasr Al-Aini School of Medicine. He was graduated with the rank of Yüzbaşi, later on the Hakimbaşi of the “Department of the Franchise diseases” (syphilis) and physiology. Later, he took over the responsibilities of treating scabies and tineas among soldiers in Al-Qasr Al-Aini hospital [16]. Abd al-Rahman al-Hawari Bey (Died 1906) Studied at Qasr al-Aini School of Medicine. After completing his medical studies, he traveled to France in 1847 and returned in 1855. Upon his return, he was appointed professor of physiology and skin diseases at the school and became the school’s vice dean in 1880 [17]. After the death of M. Ali, missions continued during the reign of Khedive Abbas I (1848–1854) to various countries such as Italy and Austria based on the advice of the British Consul!! The School of Medicine was closed during his reign and then reopened with the return of Clot Bey (1855–1856) for a very short period. During the reign of Khedive Saïd Pasha (1854–1863), the ‘second medical mission’ was sent to Austria in 1862, and its destination was changed from Austria to France in 1863 during the reign of Khedive Ismaïl Pasha (1863–1879). In this mission, two students (H. Mahmoud and M. Salem), took over the specialty of syphilitic and skin diseases [18]. Hassan Mahmoud Shaltut Pasha (1841–1906) Born in Talbieh (Giza). He completed his medical studies, at “Saint Louis” Hospital in Paris in 1869, and presented his thesis about ‘Monographie du Pemphigus’ under the supervision of Dr. Hardy (Fig. 1). He obtained a baccalaureate degree in medicine, which is equivalent in Egypt to a bachelor’s degree. He published many books and articles, including: (a) Treatise on pemphigus. (b) Modern exploration of the Egyptian abscess 1873. (c) Medical benefits in skin diseases, published in 1875. (d) Body healing in the Helwan Baths, published in 1877. He published more than 25 articles eg., on pus, hemorrhoids, dengue fever, and cholera, in Al-Muqtaf magazine, which denote that he was interested in health problems and had a message to enlighten doctors, medical field personnel, and citizens.Figure 1: Front page of M. Hassan thesis, ‘Monographie du Pemphigus’.The Egyptian Gazette issue No. 832 of October 19, 1879, mentioned him: ‘The appointment of Dr. Hassan Bey Mahmoud, Egyptian Health Inspector, A.H., took over the management of the Health Council and the Karantina administration in Alexandria ‘. As such, Dr. H. Mahmoud saved Egypt from the plague epidemic in 1881. Later, he was appointed head of the School of Medicine (1889–1891) and obtained the rank of Pasha. He was a member in two medical societies, eg., the Brazilian Medical Academy and he remained in touch with them even after his return to Egypt. He was assigned to several medical conferences as well. Dr. Hassan Mahmoud Pasha was self-taught since his birth [18]. Mohammed Salem Bey (1843–1894) Son of the late Salem Bey Ali, the health inspector of Upper Egypt, during the reign of Khedive Saïd Pasha. He completed his medical studies at the University of Paris in 1870 and wrote his medical thesis under the supervision of Dr. Fournier. Its title was about chancres: “Syphilitic chancre versus simple chancre” (Fig. 2). His training took place in ‘Lourcine’ and ‘Midi’ hospitals in Paris. Both hospitals were venereal disease hospitals, for women, men, and nanies. After his return in 1870, he was appointed to the General Canal Hospital in the Suez Canal region, then to Upper Egypt. He participated in the war with the Egyptian army in Darfur, Sudan in 1875, Ethiopian war in 1876, and alongside the Ottoman army in the war against Russia in the year 1877. The Egyptian Gazette Issue No. 763 dated June 2, 1878, mentioned that he obtained the Medal of Honor; fourth class; as at 4 G Bayada, in the first division. He was the army’s first doctor until the Orabi revolution, then a teacher at Al-Qasr Al-Aini School, and his treatise about chancres, was taught as part of Al-Qasr Al-Aini curriculum [19].Figure 2: Front page of M. Salem thesis, ‘Étude Comparative des Chancres; chancre simple et chancre syphlitique.Mohammad Radouan (1845–1920) In 1865, the Governor of Egypt, Khedive Ismail Pasha, approved the mission of M. Radouan based on the recommendation of the ‘Hajj princes’, as he worked faithfully with the pilgrims’ caravans to avoid the transmission of the cholera epidemic from Mecca to Egypt. He traveled to France and studied medicine from 1867 to 1870 [20]. He decided to complete his studies to obtain a doctorate in the field of dermatology from the year 1870 to 1875. The title of his thesis was ‘Étude Théorique et Pratique sur L’Éczema’ (Fig. 3). Dr. Hardy was the supervisor of his thesis. His studies took place at Saint Louis Hospital in Paris, one of the most famous teaching hospitals in France and the world at that time. Later, Prof. Dr. Hardy held the first international conference on dermatology in August 1989. This was in the hall of the Dermatology Wax Museum in “Saint Louis”.Figure 3: Front page of M. Radouan thesis ‘Étude Théorique et Pratique sur L’Éczema’Upon his return in 1875, Dr. M. Radouan worked and teach in Al-Qasr Al-Aini Clinic, in addition to the Khedive clinics in Cairo. In 1882, the British colonized Egypt. They tightened their control over the medical school, which led to a decrease in the number of students, and they taught medicine in the English language. They imposed annual tuition fees after free education, which led to a rapid deterioration in the conditions of the medical school, a decrease in the number of Egyptian doctors, and the restriction of entry to the medical school and medical professions to a selected handful who were skilled in English. The British colonial regime always relied on this policy to tighten its control over countries in all fields. Professor Dr. Portocalis Bey (20th century) There is no information except what he mentioned about himself. Former professor at the Sultan High College in Asetana (Istanbul). He launched a private clinic at 4 Al Mahdi Street in downtown Cairo, which is a stone’s throw from ‘Clot Bek’ Street, the red zone in Cairo, which was famous for the presence of national prostitutes and brothel houses. ‘ Clot Bek’ st. was next to the lodgment of foreign prostitutes in the ‘Azbakeya’ wealthy neighborhood district. Prof Dr. Portocalis Bey advertised himself and his clinic on daily basis in ‘Al-Ahram’ newspaper, one of the major and most widespread newspapers at the time (Fig. 4).Figure 4: Advertisement for Prof. Dr. Portocalis in Al-Ahram Newspaper.He published seven books, only one them is available at the National Egyptian libraries entitled: ‘Prostitution or the Danger of Fornication in the Egyptian Country’. Translated into Arabic by ‘Daoud Bey Barakat’ in 1907 [21]. Perhaps, Portocalis private clinic was the first private venereology clinic in Egypt. The emergence of private clinics took place from two clinics in 1925 to 39 clinics in 1949. Dr. Fakhry Mikhaïl Farag (20th century) He mentioned that his private clinic is located at 81 Abbas Street (Ramses Street) in Cairo, near the Red Zone and downtown Cairo. He studied venereology in Berlin around 1917 [22]. He published two books on venereal diseases [23], to be in the curriculum of teaching at Fouad I University (Al-Qasr Al-Aini) for many academic years starting from 1921. Prof. Dr. Abdel Moneim Al-Mufti was one of his students (personal communication). Dr. Fakhry also published a 155-page report in 1924 that he submitted to “King Fouad” I and to the Egyptian government entitled: ‘The spread of prostitution and venereal diseases in the Egyptian country and some methods that can be followed to combat them’ [24], Dr. Fakhry proposed the following: (a) The necessity of abolishing the official prostitution system, which is required by the Islamic religion, the country’s official religion. (b) The necessity of learning medicine in the Arabic language and he published his books in Arabic, except for medical terminology in Latin and Greek words. (c) The necessity of establishing a private hospital for venereal diseases in Egypt, like what exists in European countries, based on what he witnessed and experienced during his studies in Berlin. Dr. Fakhri inspected three venereal diseases office belonging to the Public Health Authority, in 1921: (a) Darb Al-Nubi office (b) Abbasiya Office. (c) Sayeda Zeinab’s office. Dr. Fakhry accurately described how antagonistic the relationship between doctors and prostitutes was. Doctors did not provide care nor time for prostitutes, Negligence was the predominant feature, and the bottom line is that there is no benefit from this medical supervision. On the contrary, he described the venereal diseases clinic in Berlin in detail. He described the examination chairs, microscopes, and the workforce. Venereal disease clinics in Berlin provided service during the morning and evening period. Thirty VD clinics existed in Berlin in 1917. Syphilis was endemic in Egypt, as such, the number of public venereal clinics and hospitals reached about 40 and perhaps more in 1949. It is worth mentioning that the books used in the curriculum of venereal and skin diseases in the 19th century at A-Qasr Al-Aini Medical School [25]: (a) Maladies de la peau ‘Rayer et Cazenave’ traduit par Ahmed Raschidi, 4 volumes. (b) Manuel des maladies Vénériennes par Philippe Ricord (1800–1889), traduit par Mustafa El Ouati, 1 volume. (c) Salem. M, Étude comparative des chancres: chancre simple et chancre syphilitique. Thesis for the doctorate in Medicine, Paris, 1870. Financial support and sponsorship Nil. Conflicts of interest There are no conflicts of interest.

title: Editorial: Microbial interactions: from mechanisms to applications in the fight against antimicrobial resistance
abstract: Microbial communities are dynamic and interconnected systems in which interactions among microorganisms shape their structure, behavior, survival, and ecological success. These interactions can promote cooperation, and collective resistance, but can also be shaped by competition in the form of antagonism, amensalism, predation and cheating among its members (Faust and Raes 2012).Understanding the molecular mechanisms and ecological principles underlying these processes (from cooperative interactions such as quorum sensing (QS), adhesion, and cross-feeding to competitive mechanisms involving antagonism and bacteriocin production) is essential for identifying new opportunities to modulate microbial communities and control pathogenicity. This knowledge is relevant in the context of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), where the widespread misuse of antibiotics has accelerated the emergence of multidrug-resistant pathogens while the lack of innovation in the development of new antibiotics has further limited available treatment options. Together, these challenges underscore the need for innovative strategies that target microbial behavior and interactions rather than bacterial viability alone (Santos et al., 2026). Considering the growing threat of AMR, the Research Topic "Microbial Interactions: from Mechanisms to Applications in the Fight Against Antimicrobial Resistance" brings contributions exploring microbial communication in the form of QS and quorum quenching interactions, biofilm formation and disruption, AMR, stress responses, gene regulation, and antivirulence strategies. Emphasis is placed on understanding intercellular signaling and developing approaches capable of disarming pathogens while minimizing the selective pressure that drives the emergence and dissemination of AMR. Together, the contributions to this collection illustrate the complexity of microbial interactions and highlight how a deeper understanding of these processes can provide both fundamental insights and new avenues for controlling resistant microorganisms.The Research Topic collected 14 papers and for the purpose of this Editorial, they were grouped into three core themes as follows: Thematic group 1 -Molecular epidemiology, resistomes, predominating during the early study period, followed by a marked shift toward the high-risk ST171 lineage. The resistance landscape was dominated by metallo-β-lactamase genes, particularly blaNDM-5 (55.3%) and blaNDM-1 (39.0%), while all isolates showed high-level resistance to meropenem and imipenem. Whole-genome analysis further revealed that IncX3 was the predominant plasmid replicon (69.9%) and was strongly associated with blaNDM-5, with all 68 blaNDM-5positive isolates carrying IncX3 plasmids. Core-genome SNP analysis identified highly related isolates, providing evidence of recent clonal transmission. Conjugation experiments confirmed horizontal transfer of blaNDM-1-and blaNDM-5-carrying plasmids in several isolates, with acquisition of these plasmids conferring markedly increased carbapenem MICs in the recipient strain.These findings indicate that the regional dissemination of CRECC is driven by both the expansion of high-risk E. hormaechei clones and the horizontal spread of blaNDM through IncX3 plasmids, highlighting the combined importance of clonal transmission and mobile resistance determinants in the persistence of carbapenem resistance.Still on the AMR at the clinical setting, Xiong et al. ( 2026) investigated six clinical isolates of the emerging multidrug-resistant pathogen Elizabethkingia anophelis recovered from hospitalized patients in Shanghai. This nosocomial pathogen is usually transmitted by contaminated medical devices causing infections like bacteremia, meningitis and pneumonia that are usually overlooked by conventional diagnostics in addition to being hard to treat. Using hybrid Illumina/PacBio WGS in combination with antimicrobial susceptibility testing and comparative genomics, the authors identified extensive resistance to β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, carbapenems, and aminoglycosides, reflecting five major resistance mechanisms: antibiotic efflux, target alteration, antibiotic inactivation, target replacement, and reduced membrane permeability. Phylogenetic analysis separated the isolates into two distinct clusters, with one group showing closer relationships to East and Southeast Asian strains and the other displaying affinities with isolates from geographically diverse origins, suggesting phylogenetic divergence and potentially independent introduction events. The isolates also carried a diverse repertoire of virulence determinants. Notably, despite their extensive drug resistance, all six isolates remained susceptible to minocycline (MIC ≤ 1 μg/mL), indicating a potential therapeutic option. The particularly distinctive genomic profile of strain EA5, including differences in resistanceand virulence-associated genes, highlights the heterogeneity of E. anophelis and the critical role of genome-level characterization in surveillance and clinical practice.Moving on to a work that compared completely different scenarios, Krämer et al. (2026) examined whether the distinct selective pressures of everyday and extreme human-built environments shape bacterial resistance by comparing isolates recovered from high-touch surfaces in German schools and on the International Space Station (ISS). As part of the "Touching Surfaces" experiment, the authors characterized Staphylococcus spp. and Micrococcus luteus isolates for antibiotic susceptibility and tolerance to spaceflight-relevant stressors, including prolonged desiccation, X-ray irradiation, and hydrogen peroxide exposure. Contrary to the expectation that the ISS environment might select for enhanced resistance, space-derived isolates did not show an overall increase in antibiotic resistance, desiccation tolerance, or X-ray resistance compared with terrestrial isolates. Both ISS and school isolates of Staphylococcus showed increased survival following hydrogen peroxide treatment relative to their corresponding type strains, while isolates of M. luteus from both environments exhibited enhanced early-stage biofilm formation. Notably, S. epidermidis from the school environment also showed increased biofilm formation, highlighting that everyday human-built environments can select for traits relevant to persistence and biofilm-associated infections. Overall, the findings suggest that extreme environments such as the ISS do not necessarily drive broad increases in bacterial resistance, but that human-built environments can select for persistenceassociated traits, emphasizing the importance of habitat-specific surveillance of microbial adaptation.Thematic Group 2: Social Dynamics, Quorum Sensing, and Transcriptional Regulation This group of articles focuses on the biochemical, genetic, and social networks that govern how bacteria communicate, coordinate stress responses/gene expression, and share protective resources. These studies span AMR at the community level, including the role of "public goods" which are shared by producing and non-producing organisms, the effect of sub-inhibitory concentrations of antibiotics over time on QS-regulated phenotypes and adaptation, as well as the description of a previously underexplored QS system in Rhodococcus erythropolis and an uncharacterized MarR-family transcriptional regulator in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.The work by Wang et al. ( 2026) is a review of the social interactions AMR at the community level. It addresses cooperative-antibiotic resistance (CoopAR), beyond biofilms, as a community-level phenomenon in which resistant bacteria protect susceptible or less-resistant neighbors by modifying the local environment or bacterial physiology. The authors examine a broader range of extracellular "public goods," including antibiotic-degrading enzymes such as β-lactamases, chloramphenicol acetyltransferase, outer membrane vesicles, metabolites, and signaling molecules, which can reduce local antibiotic concentrations and create protective microenvironments. Importantly, these benefits can extend beyond the producing cells, allowing susceptible "cheaters" to survive antibiotic exposure without bearing the metabolic cost of producing the protective factors, thereby generating complex social and eco-evolutionary dynamics. The work also emphasizes that many of these mechanisms can operate in planktonic and polymicrobial communities and that the genes encoding extracellular resistance factors may undergo horizontal transfer, potentially spreading cooperative resistance across species. The authors argue that antibiotic resistance should be considered not only as individuals' genetic traits but also as a collective property of microbial communities, with important implications for the design of antimicrobial strategies that target or disrupt these cooperative interactions.Acinetobacter baumannii, Jiang et al. (2026) showed how these responses are regulated by QS. The authors used a ΔabaI mutant of A. baumannii, which is deficient in producing acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL) QS-signaling molecules. The abaI encodes the autoinducer synthase AbaI, a homolog of the classical LuxI-synthase found in LuxI/LuxR QS-systems in Gram-negative bacteria. Using the wild-type strain and an isogenic ΔabaI mutant, together with a seven-day meropenem evolution experiment, the authors showed that sub-MIC antibiotic pressure increased the meropenem MIC of the wild-type strain from 1 to 8 μg/mL, whereas the QS-deficient mutant showed a smaller increase (0.5 to 1 μg/mL). Meropenem exposure also enhanced surface motility, biofilm formation, adhesion to and invasion of A549 epithelial cells, and virulence in Galleria mellonella in the wild-type, whereas most of these adaptive responses were substantially impaired following abaI deletion.Complementation or exogenous addition of AHLs restored several of these phenotypes. susceptibility to oxidative stress and to the cell wall-targeting antibiotic isoniazid, whereas deletion of ms_1492 produced changes in cell-envelope permeability, lipid composition, and ATP synthesis and conferred mild tolerance to H2O2 and isoniazid. Omics analyses revealed extensive alterations in lipid metabolism, including changes in multiple classes of polar lipids, while electrophoretic mobility shift assays demonstrated that Rv0737 and Ms_1492 directly bind the promoter of the sigL-rslA operon, which encodes an alternative sigma factor and its anti-sigma factor. Further expression analyses showed that Rv0737/Ms_1492 positively regulates this operon and influences downstream genes involved in lipid and fatty-acid metabolism. Together, the findings establish a direct regulatory connection between a MarR-family transcription factor and the SigL-regulatory pathway, linking transcriptional control to cell-envelope lipid remodeling, membrane permeability, oxidative-stress responses, bacterial growth, and isoniazid tolerance. The study therefore illustrates how intracellular regulatory networks can coordinate multiple physiological traits relevant to antimicrobial adaptation and identifies the Rv0737-SigL axis as a potential target for strategies against drug-resistant tuberculosis.This final translationally focused group of articles highlights innovative, target-specific approaches designed to disable biofilms, harness molecular synergies, and exploit bacterial physiological vulnerabilities. 2026) investigated whether QS-regulated metabolites produced by Pseudomonas aeruginosa can potentiate conventional antibiotics against multidrug-resistant bacteria. Using metabolites obtained from P. aeruginosa strain MC9 and identified by mass-spectrometry as pyocyanin, rhamnolipids, 4-hydroxy-2heptylquinoline (PQS), and its precursor 2-heptyl-3-hydroxy-4(1H)-quinolone (HHQ), the authors evaluated their individual antimicrobial activity and their ability to enhance the activity of conventional antibiotics against clinical isolates of Salmonella Typhimurium, Salmonella Typhi, and Escherichia coli. Although PQS and HHQ showed no direct inhibitory activity against the tested Enterobacteriaceae at concentrations up to 5 mg/mL, all four QSassociated metabolites enhanced the activity of selected antibiotics at much lower concentrations.Pyocyanin produced the strongest effect, increasing the inhibition zone by 300% when combined with sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim against S. Typhimurium, while HHQ increased the inhibition zone by 257% when combined with ampicillin against E. coli. Rhamnolipids and PQS also produced substantial synergistic effects with ceftriaxone and amoxicillin/clavulanate, respectively, and growthcurve experiments confirmed dose-dependent suppression of bacterial growth for the most effective combinations. These findings reveal that P. aeruginosa QS metabolites can have biological activities extending beyond intercellular signaling and may function as antibiotic-potentiating agents, providing a striking example of how microbial signaling molecules can be repurposed to enhance conventional antimicrobial therapy against resistant bacteria. However, as the authors emphasize, the underlying mechanisms and the safety of using such metabolites require further investigation before therapeutic application. Tareau et al. (2026) studied the anti-biofilm potential of Stigmurin, an antimicrobial peptide originally identified in the venom of the scorpion Tityus stigmurus, together with six lysine-enriched synthetic analogs designed to modify the peptide's physicochemical and structural properties.Although neither Stigmurin nor its analogs significantly inhibited the growth of P. aeruginosa or prevented biofilm formation under the conditions tested, several peptides were able to disrupt preestablished biofilms at concentrations that did not affect bacterial viability, indicating a predominantly non-bactericidal mechanism. In static assays, Stigmurin reduced mature biofilm biomass by approximately 47% after 24 h, while StigA8 and StigA16 achieved reductions of approximately 39% and 38%, respectively, at 10 μM. StigA31 analog retained substantial activity at nanomolar concentrations. In agreement with the biofilm assays, microscopy studies showed marked reductions in biofilm biovolume and average thickness after treatment under both static and dynamic flow conditions. Structural analyses by NMR revealed that StigA31 adopts an amphipathic α-helical conformation, and its activity was associated with changes in the biofilm matrix rather than stimulation of pyocyanin production. Stigmurin itself altered bacterial membrane fluidity, whereas StigA31 appeared to act through a distinct mechanism that may be related to its peptide conformation.The study demonstrates that rational modification of a natural venom-derived peptide can generate compounds capable of disrupting mature biofilms without exerting strong bactericidal pressure, highlighting peptide-based biofilm dispersal as a promising strategy for addressing persistent infections and complementing conventional antimicrobial approaches. Keshavarz et al. (2026) evaluate two synthetic derivatives of the human cathelicidin LL37, FK13a1-NH2 and KR12-NH2, against three periodontal bacteria, Fusobacterium nucleatum, Porphyromonas gingivalis, and Streptococcus oralis, under conditions that mimic cigarette smoke exposure. Both peptides inhibited planktonic P. gingivalis and F. nucleatum, with KR12-NH2 showing particularly strong activity against P. gingivalis: the combination of 500 μg/mL KR12-NH2 with 50% cigarette smoke extract (CSE) produced 98% inhibition of P. gingivalis growth, indicating that tobacco exposure did not compromise its antimicrobial activity. Checkerboard experiments showed that the interaction between KR12-NH2 and CSE was pronounced against P. gingivalis, whereas the effects against the other species were more variable. In addition, both peptides significantly reduced the thickness of established single-species biofilms, although their effects were considerably less pronounced in complex multispecies biofilms. Overall, the study demonstrates that LL37-derived peptides can retain substantial antimicrobial and anti-biofilm activity under tobacco-associated conditions, suggesting that environmental conditions can unexpectedly modulate the efficacy of antimicrobial peptides. These findings support the potential of synthetic LL37 derivatives as alternatives or complement to conventional antibiotics in periodontal infections, particularly in the clinically relevant context of smoking. Wickham et al. (2026) investigate whether the transient newly released (NRel) phenotype, previously observed after reagent-mediated biofilm disruption, can also be induced through rapid physical disruption. Across four clinically relevant pathogens, non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHI), methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Streptococcus pneumoniae, the authors show that rapid mechanical disruption, including pipetting, sonication, scraping, and vortexing, releases biofilm-resident cells that become markedly more susceptible to antibiotics than their planktonic counterparts. The effect was also reproduced in NTHI using a cationic-depletion approach, demonstrating that NRel induction is not dependent on a particular chemical reagent. NRel phenotype was characterized by three coordinated features: enhanced antibiotic susceptibility, a transient time-dependent response, and a distinctive geneexpression profile. In NTHI, the authors further show that antibiotic sensitivity changes rapidly after release, consistent with a physiological transition rather than a stable genetic alteration, while qRT-PCR confirmed differential expression of previously identified NRel-associated genes. The authors propose that the rate of biofilm disruption is the critical determinant, because cells released abruptly from the protective biofilm environment may not have sufficient time to activate the physiological programs required for survival in the planktonic state. Thus, rather than simply removing the physical barrier of the biofilm, rapid disruption appears to temporarily place bacterial cells in a vulnerable physiological state that can be exploited therapeutically, providing a potential strategy for converting biofilm-associated antibiotic tolerance into antibiotic susceptibility.Regarding the use of bioactive compound combinations, Chen et al. ( 2026) investigated the synergistic antibiofilm activity of sodium fluoride (NaF) and the green tea polyphenol epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) against Streptococcus mutans, integrating omics analyses to elucidate the mechanisms underlying their combined effects. Checkerboard assays identified an effective low-dose combination of 62.5 ppm fluoride and 0.5 mg/mL EGCG, which produced more than 90% inhibition of biofilm formation with a fractional inhibitory concentration (FIC) index of 0.5, indicating synergy. The combination markedly reduced biofilm biomass and viable cells while disrupting microcolony organization and decreasing water-insoluble extracellular polysaccharide (EPS) production, although the reduction in EPS was not always proportional to the reduction in total biofilm biomass, suggesting additional mechanisms beyond matrix disruption. title: Toxic and Metabolic Disorders of the Nervous System
abstract: A. Folate and Vitamin B12 Deficiencies (see Chapter 20) B. Vitamin E Deficiency (see Chapter 9) 1. Associated with a. Cystic fibrosis in children b. Severe malabsorption because of disease of the alimentary tract c. Inherited conditions, including ataxia with isolated vita- min E deficiency (due to mutation of α-tocopherol transfer protein gene on chromosome 8q) or abetalipoproteinemia (see Chapter 9) 2. Vitamin E: radical scavenger and antioxidant 3. Clinical features: spinocerebellar syndrome (cerebellar ataxia and large-fiber sensory loss), areflexia, ataxic dysarthria, cerebellar and sensory gait ataxia, extensor plantar responses, acanthocytosis, hemolytic anemia, retinitis pigmentosa 4. Pathology: acanthocytosis (peripheral blood smear); swollen axons in affected central nervous system (CNS) structures, including posterior columns C. Niacin (nicotinic acid) Deficiency (pellagra) 1. Niacin a. Nicotinic acid and nicotinamide (latter is readily deaminated in the body to form nicotinic acid) b. Nicotinic acid and nicotinamide form nicotinamide adenosine dinucleotide (NAD+) and NAD phosphate (NADP+), important coenzymes in carbohydrate metabolism c. Niacin is derived from enriched grains and cereals, milk, meat and, in small quantities, as end product of tryptophan metabolism 2. Prevalence of pellagra has decreased with fortification of bread and cereals with niacin 3. Nonendemic pellagra may occur in context of alcoholism or nutritional deficiency due to gastrointestinal tract disease 4. Clinical triad of “3Ds”: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia 5. Gastrointestinal features: stomatitis, diarrhea, abdomi- nal pain, vomiting 6. Neurologic: myelopathy and spastic paraparesis, irri- tability, depression, apathy, memory loss 7. Dermatitis: hyperkeratotic, hyperpigmented, diffuse, extensive rash 8. Treatment: oral or parenteral nicotinic acid or nicotinamide D. Vitamin B6 1. Vitamin B6: pyridoxine, pyridoxal, pyridoxamine-all are precursors of coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate 2. Ubiquitous in corn, wheat, egg yolk, and lean meat 3. Clinical syndrome of deficiency a. Infantile onset 1) Occurs in setting of syndrome of pyridoxine deficiency- related seizures (due to malnutrition of mothers) or congenital dependency on pyridoxine (not true deficiency) (see Chapter 12) 2) Normal prenatal and peripartum course, followed by poor feeding, irritability, exaggerated startle, and abrupt onset of seizures (may be intractable and lead to status epilepticus) b. Adult onset 1) Rare: adults are much more resistant to vitamin B6 deficiency 2) Often due to intake of isoniazid, hydralazine, or penicillamine 3) Distal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy (predomi- nant features of sensory symptoms and axonal degeneration) 4) Treatment: slow improvement with withdrawal of offending drug or initiation of low-dose vitamin B6 supplementation 5) Primary prevention: coadministration of vitamin B6 prevents this neuropathy 4. Pyridoxine excess a. Sensory polyneuropathy: length-dependent axonal neuropathy with predominant features of sensory loss or sensory ataxia due to polyganglionopathy (see Chapter 21) b. Partial or complete resolution with withdrawal of offending agent E. Vitamin A 1. Hypervitaminosis A (vitamin A toxicity) may cause a. Pseudotumor cerebri b. Birth defects and pervasive developmental disorders in children born to mothers with this condition 2. Vitamin A deficiency: rare, may present with night blindness F. Thiamine Deficiency 1. Most frequently occurs in setting of alcoholism 2. Thiamine is a precursor for the biologically active thi- amine pyrophosphate 3. Thiamine pyrophosphate acts as a coenzyme for a. Transketolase reaction in hexose monophosphate shunt b. Oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to form acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) by pyruvate dehydrogenase c. Conversion of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl CoA by α- ketoglutarate dehydrogenase 4. Thiamine requirements are greatest during periods of high metabolic demand and/or high glucose intake: this may partly explain occurrence of Wernicke’s encephalopathy with administration of intravenous glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient 5. Beriberi a. Length-dependent, axonal, sensorimotor peripheral neu- ropathy with distal sensory loss, paresthesias, weakness (termed “dry beriberi” in absence of cardiac involvement) b. Associated with cardiac involvement: cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, congestive heart failure (termed “wet beriberi”) c. Laboratory diagnosis 1) Decreased serum and urine levels of thiamine 2) Decreased erythrocyte transketolase activity (functional assay) 3) Increased serum pyruvate levels 4) Electromyographic evidence of axonal, distal periph- eral neuropathy 6. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (see Chapter 7) G. Other Nervous System Conditions Associated With Alcoholism 1. Alcoholic neuropathy a. Associated with severe, prolonged alcohol use b. Predominantly sensory neuropathy: painful neuropathy, painful dysesthesias, paresthesias, allodynia c. Weakness is mild, usually involves distal lower extremity d. Autonomic involvement e. Predisposition to compression mononeuropathies f. Associated with other alcohol-related complications: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and cerebellar degeneration g. Patients should receive parenteral thiamine supplementation 2. Ethanol-induced myopathy a. Usually develops in setting of chronic, heavy ethanol intake and binge drinking b. Occurs as acute necrotizing myopathy or chronic myopathy with muscle wasting c. Acute necrotizing myopathy 1) Acute onset of myonecrosis, often in the midst of heavy bout of drinking (in context of chronic alcoholism) 2) Acute onset of muscle pain and myoedema, often associated with myoglobinuria 3) Weakness: often proximal and symmetric or there may be focal weakness of the quadriceps or calves 4) Pathology: patchy, segmental necrotizing process, with degeneration and regeneration of the muscle fibers d. Chronic alcoholic myopathy 1) Gradual onset and progression of proximal weakness, muscle wasting, cramps, and myalgias 2) Increased serum levels of creatine kinase and myoglobinuria 3. Marchiafava-Bignami disease (see Chapter 7) 4. Alcoholic dementia (see Chapter 7) 5. Acute withdrawal syndrome, including delirium tremens and alcohol withdrawal seizures 6. Alcohol-related cerebellar degeneration a. Usually in context of long-standing alcohol abuse b. Insidious and gradual onset and progression of cerebellar ataxia c. Often associated with alcoholic neuropathy and with- drawal seizures d. Abstinence may yield improvement: gradual, often incomplete e. Pathology 1) Cerebellar atrophy: predilection for anterior and superior vermis 2) Diffuse loss of Purkinje cells, patchy loss of granule cells 3) Often concomitant diffuse cerebral atrophy 7. Fetal alcohol syndrome a. Occurs in infants whose mothers drink alcohol during pregnancy: most afflicted infants are born to mothers with alcohol-related complications during pregnancy, but there is no minimum safe amount of alcohol intake during the gestational period; expectant mothers must abstain completely b. Intrauterine growth retardation: low birth weight, small head circumference c. Craniofacial and joint deformities d. Congenital developmental malformations of brain, including microcephaly, agenesis of corpus callosum, cerebellar dysplasia, heterotopic gray matter e. Afflicted infants: irritability, poor feeding f. High infant mortality rate: 1 in 6 afflicted infants die g. Many infants who survive infancy have psychomotor developmental delay, mental retardation, and pervasive developmental disorders marked by poor learning, memory, attention, and problem solving; social and behavioral problems H. Copper Deficiency 1. Acquired (see Chapter 20) 2. Congenital: Menke syndrome I. Postgastroplasty Polyneuropathy 1. Associated with jejunoileal bypass, gastrojejunectomy, gastric stapling, gastroplasty, gastrectomy with Rouxen-Y anastomosis 2. Neurologic syndrome always follows intractable vomiting and precipitous weight loss 3. Acute or subacute onset of symmetric sensory loss and paresthesias, distal and/or proximal weakness, which may progress to quadriparesis 4. Few patients develop encephalopathy A. Metal Intoxication 1. Arsenic a. Usually associated with deliberate poisoning, may also occur in the context of accidental exposure b. Shortly after ingestion, arsenic is stored in reticuloendothelial system, kidney, and intestines; is slowly released c. Slow excretion via kidney and feces d. Deposited in hair within 2 weeks; remains in the hair for years e. Clinical features vary, depending on the dose 1) Acute or subacute exposure: abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, hyperthermia, headaches, anxiety, vertigo, possibly seizures, encephalopathy, and coma (if severe) 2) Fatal acute poisoning: precipitous development of lethargy and coma, followed by death in few days, may be due to diffuse edema and/or hemorrhagic encephalopathy 3) Low-dose chronic exposure: similar clinical features but much less severe; abdominal pain, vertigo, longstanding cognitive disturbance, persistent headaches, and development of peripheral neuropathy 4) Sphincter dysfunction 5) Optic neuropathy: possible delayed manifestation 6) Mees’ lines: white lines in nails, usually appear 2 to 3 weeks after acute exposure 7) Peripheral neuropathy a) Painful, distal peripheral neuropathy (axonopathy) b) Distal pansensory loss in a glove-stocking distribu- tion involving both small-fiber and large-fiber modalities and causing dense proprioceptive loss and pseudoathetosis, reduced temperature sensation, hyperesthesia, dysesthesia, and allodynia c) Weakness involving the distal extremity, hand, and foot muscles: effort may be poor because of dense proprioceptive loss d) Hyporeflexia or areflexia distally e) Associated with exfoliative dermatitis f. Diagnosis 1) 24-Hour urine heavy metal arsenic levels: may be falsely elevated by ingestion of shellfish 2) Increased arsenic levels in nail clippings or pubic hair (preferable to scalp hair because of less chance of environmental contamination) g. Treatment 1) Acute treatment: supportive measures, including hydration and morphine for abdominal pain, gastric lavage 2) Chelation therapy with dimercaprol or its water-soluble derivative, dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA); or penicillamine (best if started early) 2. Inorganic lead a. Toxicity due to occupational or nonoccupational expo- sure or, in children, old lead-based paint b. Lead inhibits erythrocyte γ-aminolevulinic acid dehy- dratase in biochemical pathways of porphyrin metabolism c. Children 1) Acute intoxication: acute gastrointestinal illness, confusion, lethargy, seizures, coma, and respiratory arrest with high levels of exposure 2) Chronic, low-level exposure: gradual onset of listlessness, behavioral changes, psychomotor slowing, sleep disturbance, seizures, gait disorder characterized by clumsiness or frank ataxia d. Adults 1) Polyneuropathy: predominantly motor neuropathy, with distal weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations (pain uncommon) 2) Motor manifestation may be more prominent in upper extremities: may present with bilateral wristdrop, with or without distal lower limb weakness 3) Motor neuropathy commonly involves radial nerve (wristdrop is most common) 4) There may or may not be sensory symptoms, predominantly paresthesias (allodynia and dysesthesias are uncommon) e. Laboratory diagnosis 1) Microcytic, hypochromic anemia 2) Basophilic stippling of red blood cells on peripheral blood smear 3) Renal insufficiency, azotemia 4) Elevated blood and urine levels of lead f.
